Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 3.07 ± 0.21. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Namely, we consider models featuring a vast web of cosmic filaments and a significant magnetic field intensity, as well as models depicting cosmic structures and magnetic field fluctuations within the host galaxy, although these the latter may require further study. Our research at the Pierre Auger Observatory underscores the importance of large-scale anisotropy studies in cosmic-ray astrophysics. To further explore these anisotropies, the observatory's successor, the Pierre Auger Upgrade, and magnetic detection systems in next-generation experiments, such as the Square Kilometre Array, will need to surpass a level of sensitivity beyond that achieved with our current study. Quantum mechanical systems associated with semisimple Lie algebras can be examined using noncommutative quantum mechanics. In this analysis, we discuss the spectrum problem for a specific su(2) representation, applying deformed coordinates. Furthermore, we establish the equivalence between the deformed Hamiltonian and its unmodified form, demonstrating the utility of noncommutative quantum mechanics for analyzing Lie algebra-based systems. Additionally, we explore potential generalizations of this approach. Next, we analyze the time-evolution operator's behavior in its deformed state. Lastly, we consider various deformed configurations. Finally, we examine three specific su(2) representations. 

In the first instance, we consider a rung-like su(2) representation, demonstrating the time-evolution operator's periodic behavior and correlated base changes within the operator's eigenstate. We then move on to analyze two non-rungetic su(2) representations. Notably, we observe periodic behavior in the time-evolution operator for the second rungetic representation, along with associated base changes in the operator's eigenstate. Conversely, the Hamiltonian's eigenstate exhibits anti-periodic behavior in the third rungetic representation. Furthermore, we find that periodic or anti-periodic behaviors are indicative of Heisenberg-weyl group representations. 

Finally, we discuss multiple rung-like su(2) representations, demonstrating time-evolution operator periodic behavior and associated base changes in the operator's eigenstate. We also examine number-state and Glauber-state periodic or anti-periodic behaviors in all analyzed cases. Additionally, we discuss potential connections between these results and solid-state physics. 

In the case of solid-state physics, represented by Bloch bundles, we outline strategies for applying noncommutative quantum mechanics. We demonstrate time-evolution operator periodic behavior in both free particle and harmonic oscillator models. 

We also investigate superposition states' periodic or anti-periodic behavior in both analyzed cases. Moreover, we discuss potential connections between these results and discrete quantum mechanics. 

In the case of discrete quantum mechanics, we outline configurations for implementing noncommutative quantum mechanics. We demonstrate time-evolution operator periodic behavior in both finite and infinite well models. 

We also investigate superposition states' periodic or anti-periodic behavior in both analyzed cases. 

We express our gratitude to M. Moshovitz for providing valuable insights on time-evolution operator periodic behavior in both free particle and harmonic oscillator models.

Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy. Our code is openly accessible on GitHub, showcasing the versatility of this framework through multiple demonstration examples involving financial time-series forecasting, audio classification, and biosignals analysis. Our optimization framework, Pruning In Time (PIT), is now freely downloadable at https://github.com/CompVis/PIT, along with all associated demonstration codes at https://github.com/CompVis/PIT-demo, under the terms of the permissive MIT License. Our model variants achieving state-of-the-art performance in financial time-series forecasting are listed on https://github.com/CompVis/PIT/commit/af3dca3, while those for audio classification and biosignals analysis are available at https://github.com/CompVis/PIT/commit/5c0b0f5 and https://github.com/CompVis/PIT/commit/0f5f5b5, respectively. Our approach, Pruning In Time, has been successfully applied to various temporal sequence analysis tasks utilizing the lightweight and highly customizable framework introduced in this paper, known as Pruning In Time Network (PITN). PITN's architecture is outlined in detail in section 3 of this document, along with a discussion of its key features in section 4. Our demonstration examples highlighting the effectiveness of PITN are discussed in section 5, while section 6 explores the underlying reasoning behind our methodology. Furthermore, section 7 provides a comparative analysis between our method and alternative network optimization strategies. Lastly, section 8 outlines the future directions for enhancing the performance of TCNs utilizing the PITN framework. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a certain degree of solvability. Specifically, we demonstrate that for this type of algebra, the product operation can be effectively 'tamed' by a combination of its original properties and those of its subalgebra, ultimately leading to a demonstration of solvability. As a result of this proof, we also derive proof by a simpler method for a previous theorem regarding the solvability of nilpotent Zinbiel algebras. Additionally, our proof includes a demonstration of the solvability of the subalgebra generated by elements of a specific form within a larger Zinbiel algebra, characterized by a specific set of polynomial equations. This, in turn, allows for a further conclusion regarding the structure of nilpotent Zinbiel algebras. Lastly, we include a corollary regarding the structure of their finite-dimensional subalgebras. This research can be seen as a continuation of prior work by Dzhumadilla and Smith on the solvability of filiform Zinbiel algebras, demonstrating that the property of being nilpotent is equivalent, but with the added benefit of a simpler proof. This result is further generalized to apply to all finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras with a nilpotent subalgebra, providing a specific degree of solvability. This degree is specifically expressed in terms of the number of steps required for the product operation to 'cycle back' to the original element, effectively quantifying the solvability of the algebra. Finally, we include a conclusion regarding the structure of nilpotent finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebras, stating that all such algebras can be expressed as a direct sum of their nilpotent subalgebra and an abelian ideal, with the latter being isomorphic to the center of the former. The combined use of both the unified inverse relation and traditional bunched variables offers a comprehensive approach for managing implication and approximation in DLE-Logics, offering a glimpse into the potential for a more expansive relational model that encompasses both. Furthermore, this inverse relation is an operator-based construct, enabling a more abstract description of its properties and behaviour. A central aspect of this study is the identification of the unified inverse relation as an expansion of the SIOS operator, previously studied in the context of modal logic. This connection facilitates the transfer of insights from the SIOS operator research to the unified inverse relation. A key achievement of this study is the demonstration of the unified inverse relation's compatibility with the DLE-Logics semantics, built using correspondence spaces and set theory. This compatibility is proven through the application of the Scott induction principle, an established semantic technique. A significant consequence of this study is the provision of a semantic basis for evaluating the unified inverse relation in relation to other logics and operators, such as negation and implication. A key aspect of this evaluation is the examination of the unified inverse relation's interaction with the semantics of bunched variables, including its impact on the distribution of approximations and implications. Additionally, this study explores the unified inverse relation's effect on the application of the distribution law, showcasing how this interaction can result in more efficient proofs. A further consequence of this study is the identification of a variant of the unified inverse relation that is compatible with the semistructured correspondence spaces used in separation logic, paving the way for a corresponding logic. A key achievement of this study is the demonstration of the unified inverse relation's utility in a practical setting, utilizing the TAPAS theorem prover to verify the validity of the corresponding logic's axioms and proofs. The cluster's radial velocity was found to be 54.8 ± 2.4 km/s. A study of the variable stars within Ton 2 expanded existing research and identified 34 new RR Lyrae and 12 other types of pulsators and blue horizontal branch stars. The data from APOGEE-2 and CCD also provide insight into the population of the cluster and surrounding field. A turn-off point and RR Lyrae zero-age horizontal branch were used as a reference point to estimate the cluster's distance at 8.78 ± 0.12. A measurement of the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 1.63 ± 0.03 observed in the CCD data was also utilized in the analysis. When considering all available information, a cluster distance of 8.78 kpc appeared most consistent with the evidence from RR Lyrae, BHB, and the overall morphology of the field around Ton 2. A previous study from 1959 reported an incorrect distance estimate due to an inaccurate reduction of spectroscopic data. A distance of 8.78 kpc for Ton 2 is relevant as it affects previous research on the Mestel model of the Milky Way and the formation of the globular cluster field. A new estimate for the model's constant 'k' was provided and was found to be (0.0684 ± 0.0063) (R_0/8.2 kpc). A value for 'k' was derived from the observed morphology of the cluster and surrounding field and is less sensitive to the uncertainty in the cluster's distance. A value for 'k' was validated through observations of three other clusters within the APOGEE-2 sample. A value for 'k' was found to be relevant in determining the mass-to-light ratio of the Milky Way. A mass-to-light ratio of the Milky Way was calculated and found to be 3.07 ± 0.

Developed with the goal of simplifying complex many-body problems, this deep learning model uses mini-branches to quantify the effects of single electron excitations. Through a superposition of these excitations, CI-Pot can efficiently represent the full CI wavefunction. Optimized in an autoencoder framework, CI-Pot exhibits high conformity to full CI data, demonstrating excellent performance in various benchmark tests. Specifically, CI-Pot shows significant gains over traditional mean-field approaches and existing neural network ground state predictors in tests of energy accuracy. Furthermore, case studies highlight the potential of CI-Pot to drive innovation in theoretical chemistry methods, addressing challenges such as dimensionality, data privacy, and interpretability, and opening up avenues for generalized applications across diverse systems and phenomena. Overall, CI-Pot represents a crucial breakthrough in the practical application of deep learning to chemical many-body problems, providing a viable path to solving complex chemical challenges. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. In addition to developing a statistical method to identify and reject noisy data, we discovered that using more pixels (i.e., using wide-field photometry) yields a more significant reduction in estimated errors than utilizing more bandwidth does. As a result of these advancements, we were able to determine the aerosol depth with a precision of 0.01-0.04, depending on the time frame and location, and our technique has the potential to contribute usefully to monitoring the atmosphere's conditions over vast areas in the future. In order to further validate our results, we conducted further observations and obtained corresponding data with a new telescope featuring a different detector type. Despite some differences in measurement outcomes, our new technique remains capable of determining the aerosol depth with a similar level of precision. Recently, modern pose estimation techniques, particularly two-dimensional (2D) pose estimation methods, rely heavily on over-fitted models and inaccurate pose estimators, which hinders progress in estimating three-dimensional (3D) poses. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative approach, named DeepHMap++, based on the unique concept of projection clustering. This model uses dual networks to simultaneously produce a pose distribution map and a correspondence map, both guided by clustering principles. Through projection clustering, we leverage pose distribution information to refine correspondence maps, while corresponding correspondences provide prior knowledge to enhance pose distribution maps. This bidirectional learning mechanism propels the model toward finding a global minimum, and we validate its effectiveness on popular benchmark datasets. Notably, DeepHMap++ surpasses state-of-the-art 3D pose estimation models, specifically achieving superior performance on the CMU MOSEI and H36M datasets. Moreover, we observe that this approach yields pose estimates with higher completeness rates and accuracy levels. To facilitate further research, we introduce the CMU MOSEI dataset split and release DeepHMap++ models pre-trained on the H36M and CMU MOSEI datasets. Additionally, we explore the phenomenon of low-dimensional pose representation and the resulting challenges in 3D pose estimation. To address these issues, we introduce the idea of high-dimensional pose reconstruction and validate it through extensive experiments. Finally, we discuss the pros and cons of low-dimensional models and provide insights into the future directions for 3D pose estimation research. Numerical relativity simulations allow us to study how binary black hole mergers interact with their surroundings. However, these simulations start only shortly before the merger and require predetermined initial conditions to proceed. Due to the intricate formation processes of binary black holes, their environment is often thought to consist of dark matter without notable effects. Yet, existing simulations fail to account for the dynamics of dark matter during the merger. In our research, we've developed a new method for incorporating dark matter into these simulations, using a small number of initial dark matter particles whose paths are influenced by the binary black holes' gravity. We've applied this technique to various configurations of binary black holes surrounded by dark matter, observing the distribution of dark matter during the merger and verifying that it has minimal impact on the merger itself. Our approach can be used to inform semi-analytical models of binary black hole formation, and we're making our code publicly available for further research. In particular, we've considered three scenarios: mergers occurring in vacuum, systems with surrounding matter that isn't directly affected by gravity, and systems surrounded by dark matter. We've also simulated highly unequal mergers, discovering that dark matter can become entangled in the resulting jet of energy. Our research has implications for how these events appear to observers at different distances. We're currently investigating how this approach can be incorporated into larger binary black hole formation simulations. Furthermore, we're exploring ways to incorporate a larger number of dark matter particles, as well as developing new visual tools to better understand the behavior of dark matter in these mergers. Additionally, we're examining the potential for dark matter to affect the emission of gravitational waves during these events, and we're making our code publicly available for further research into the intersection of general relativity and dark matter dynamics. Researchers examined the characteristics of a new sonic lens material called HMA-Lens, comprising a layer of high-modulus acrylate gel attached to the surface of a mirror-like silicone substrate. Studies showed that this design significantly enhances photoacoustic tomography (PAT) image quality by minimizing gel-related distortions and improving spatial resolution. Compared to traditional gel-based sonic lenses, HMA-Lens offered better PAT performance with larger detectors, offering a promising solution for breast cancer imaging. Optical coherence tomography was also used to investigate the lens's surface topology and scattering properties, providing insights into its optical and acoustic properties. This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions. All data and analyses are based on direct observations of spheres entering water from above, and the resulting datasets are the basis for refined correlations between spheres' velocities and the time it takes for the surface seal to close. These velocity-time correlations will be useful in understanding other water-entry velocity regimes and potential applications in both nature and engineering.

In order to protect sensitive information from malicious attackers who have infiltrated a system, hardware-based security techniques were developed to provide a secure foundation for programs. However, even with these security measures in place, there is still the risk of software exploiting hardware vulnerabilities. To address this, this research introduces the concept of "physically-isolated" hardware, which creates separate physical environments for a system's resources, such as CPU and memory, to prevent software from exploiting hardware-based attacks. The goal of this research is to minimize the amount of trust required for programs to operate on such hardware, by assigning a program's code and data to the same physical island, and using low-level memory safety techniques to contain a program's misuse of memory. The resulting system, which is based on RISC-V and uses physically-isolated hardware, demonstrates its ability to prevent software-based attacks and reduce trust requirements. The research also evaluates the performance impact of this design, and explores ways to optimize it for real-world applications. The outcome indicates that programs with minimal security vulnerabilities experience minimal performance degradation, while those with security flaws run significantly slower and consume more energy. To put this in perspective, a web browser with certain security vulnerabilities runs at 0.4% of the speed it would on standard hardware, but on the isolated-RISC-V architecture. On the other end, optimizing programs with security flaws for the isolated architecture results in a 20-day compilation process, but after that they run at 4% of the speed they would on standard hardware. The research also shows that assigning a program's code and data to the same physical island prevents software-based attacks, but does not prevent other types of attacks, such as those that target hardware components like network interface cards. The outcome of this research has implications for the design of hardware systems, and indicates that the principle of least privilege is crucial in order to minimize the amount of trust required for programs to operate on such systems. The research also raises questions about what other types of attacks could be prevented with physically-isolated hardware, and how the performance impact of this design could be further optimized. The outcome of this research has also been incorporated into a new architecture called Octopus, which uses eight physically-isolated hardware cores, but only relies on seven of them in order to minimize the amount of trust required for programs to operate on such hardware. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor, known as $\Psi$, in accordance with the principles of conformal gravity, particularly determining the Weyl curvature index, which represents the minimum number of non-zero $\Psi$ components in a spacetime. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external fillings which can cause certain parts to be difficult to read. The cost of exploring and producing oil and gas from offshore platforms is significantly high, making it essential to implement geosteering techniques that facilitate real-time decision-making during horizontal well placement. This process involves repeatedly drilling and retrieving formation properties through the well bore for updated data, leading to extensive costs. To optimize this process, it's essential to create a model that forecasts the formation properties in the well bore and accurately predicts the uncertainties involved. By utilizing ensemble techniques with multiple models, we can better grasp the uncertainties and make more informed, data-driven decisions regarding geosteering. The approach we propose employs an ensemble of models based on the Petrel software's built-in well log analysis module, in combination with statistical modeling. This results in an ensemble of probability density functions that accurately represents the uncertainties associated with the formation properties in the well bore. By integrating this approach with the real-time data, we can update the uncertainties and make more precise predictions on the location of the well within the target formation. This, in turn, enables more effective geosteering, maximizing the chances of successfully completing the well on schedule and within budget. Through the implementation of this technique in a real-field scenario, we achieved a reduction in the uncertainty regarding the well placement by more than 2.5 times and avoided the risk of missing the target formation. This, in turn, led to a successful well completion. Additionally, this approach can be applied to other well placement applications. Furthermore, the approach we proposed is versatile and can be adapted for use with different software and models, making it a valuable solution for the oil and gas industry. This note establishes a connection between the complexity measure known as conformal field theory complexity and Euler-Arnold equations, highlighting the inherent difficulties in defining a non-local operator like the stress-energy tensor's coherent state counterpart. A specialized scenario, based on an idempotent property, yields a linearized Euler-Arnold equation that can be analyzed to understand the implications of CFT complexity in a specific context. Additionally, ZAMO (zero angular momentum vector) modes in AdS$_3$ CFT are shown to serve as a suitable framework for exploring the relationships between Euler-Arnold equations, stress-energy tensor's coherent state, and holographic complexity. Our analysis demonstrates that in this setting, the fidelity-based complexity measure aligns with the tensor density-type holographic complexity, and identifies an operator that can mediate these relationships. Furthermore, we identify potential obstacles to applying holographic complexity probes and suggest that the idempotent property may hold universally for all conformal field theories. Lastly, our findings provide a foundation for further investigating the relationships between operator, state, and geometry in conformal field theories. Moreover, we propose the term "holo-complexity" to encompass these interconnected ideas. To recognize new categories from minimal labeled data, few-shot learning has been rapidly evolving in recent years. However, traditional methods that rely on average operations for learning prototypes often struggle due to the influence of outliers. This research proposes a new prototype representation model that utilizes an exponential operator to produce compact prototypes, effectively reducing the impact of data points that are far from the prototype. Additionally, this model incorporates a prototype competition mechanism to assign a competition coefficient to each prototype, reflecting its representation quality. Through experiments on popular few-shot learning datasets, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance compared to state-of-the-art approaches. Furthermore, this research introduces the Prototype Competition Mechanism (PCM) model, which achieves remarkable success in real-world applications with large category overlaps, showcasing a notable increase in metric accuracy of up to 11.4% on miniImageNet, or 6.6% on calif-Birds. The code for the PCM model is publicly available on GitHub. Moreover, this research introduces the UC-Merge dataset, characterized by significant category overlaps, large displacement differences, and diverse data point shapes, further complicating the prototype learning process. On this dataset, the proposed PCM model surpasses baseline models by a significant margin, with a 9.6% point gap in metric accuracy. This research also explores the implications of competing prototypes on outlier detection and demonstrates that PCM's competition coefficients can effectively indicate prototypes that require re-examination due to potential data quality issues. This insight enables the cost-effective addition of reliable data points to existing categories, further enhancing the efficacy of few-shot learning in real-world settings. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these constraints and the complex, multi-sparse-domain scenario, there is a pressing need for a more comprehensive approach that considers all available domains and promotes cooperative learning to counter the sparsity challenge. To this end, we introduce a novel multi-sparse-domain CDR framework called MACAP, which leverages the information across all available domains through a collaborative learning process to enhance a comprehensive aspect preference model. By incorporating a domain-weighting mechanism and a domain-adaptive activation function, MACAP develops a more sophisticated and interpretable model that activates the inclusion of information from each domain, adapts to the unique characteristics of each domain, and prevents over-reliance on a single domain. MACAP's effectiveness is demonstrated through comprehensive experiments and practical applications, showcasing its superiority over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models and the critical role that domain quality plays in the performance of MACAP. Moreover, MACAP's robustness and practical viability are validated through an extensive analysis of sensitive factors and real-world deployment. Overall, MACAP sets a new benchmark for the field, and its code is publicly available for reference. Nonetheless, MACAP's application in real-world scenarios necessitates careful consideration of domain data protection and privacy policies. Similarly, in the Amazon Product co-purchase Network dataset, users must give their consent for the use of their purchased product history. In line with evolving data protection policies, we recommend that future CDR models, including MACAP, prioritize privacy preservation and secure collaborative learning through differential privacy and secure multi-party computation. It states that any element within a Coxeter group can be expressed as a product of a minimal length, where this product comprises subunits known as reflections. However, the foundation theorem does not generalize to the infinite Coxeter groups, or more specifically, the hyperbolic Coxeter groups. By combining the most up-to-date cosmological parameters with the Pantheon sample and the DES-SV week lensing signal, we derive a median amplification of $A(z)\simeq 1.21$ at $z=1.3$. This amplification results in an effective extension of the Pantheon sample's reach by about one-dynami cal distance bins. Furthermore, we establish a scaling relation between the amplification and redshift, with a linear fit yielding a slope of $1.08\pm 0.20$ when considering the Pantheon sample and $1.03\pm 0.26$ for a subset of the sample with reduced scatter. Our study provides evidence for the shape of the amplification's scaling relation with redshift and highlights the importance of incorporating weak lensing effects when analyzing supernovae data from higher $z$. By comparing our results with the amplification induced by the DES-SV full sample's convergence field, we discovered a smaller than expected effective lensing impact on the distance determination when considering the full set of desnv weak lensing observations. This research has relevant implications for upcoming supernovae distance determinations. On the other hand, with desnv-like weak lensing observations, the distance determinations from supernovae samples above $z \simeq 1$ will be dominated by the amplification rather than the intrinsic dimming. Consequently, when combining these analyses, the amplified intrinsic magnitude should be modeled with a cosmological constant as a function of redshift rather than a constant. This finding is particularly significant for the planning of future supernovae-weak lensing combined analyses. With desnv-like weak lensing observations, the determination of the Hubble constant will also become less robust. Additionally, we established that the amplification's scaling relation with redshift can be modeled using a simple linear or logarithmic form. This study explores the double longitudinal spin asymmetry in semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering where hadron pairs' transverse momentum is not considered. Specifically, we investigate the cause of the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in hadron production, accounting for the connection between the helicity distribution $g_1$ and the twist-3 dihadron fragmentation function. Using a spectator model, we calculate the interference term between $s$-wave and $p$-wave and estimate this asymmetry at various experiments, including COMPASS, JLab 12 GeV, and the future EIC. Our analysis suggests that the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in SIDIS can serve as a key test for the dihadron fragmentation function. Moreover, we demonstrate that this asymmetry is predominantly driven by the kick operator in the wave function, whereas in fragmentation case, it is dominated by the bump-operator. This distinction allows for a distinction between the kick and bump operators in future measurements. Additionally, we find that the kick-operator dominance holds for both SIDIS and target-spin unpolarized hadron production processes. Consequently, we derive explicit expressions for the cosine azimuthal asymmetry in these cases and estimate their magnitudes at various experiments. These predictions provide crucial guidance for the optimal design of experiments to uncover the twist-3 fragmentation function at the EIC. Furthermore, we extend our investigation to consider the cos$\phi_R$-dependent cross section in hadron production, examining not only SIDIS but also PHOTOPRODUCTION, showcasing that similar asymmetries emerge in PHOTOPRODUCTION, albeit with distinct $s$-dependent behavior, whereas SIDIS exhibits $s$-independence. Lastly, we outline the relevant subdiagram contributions in PHOTOPRODUCTION and propose that future experiments undertake a comprehensive investigation of cos$\phi_R$-dependent distributions across various processes. This paper presents a Wikipedia-based entity recommendation approach called YAHOO-WE, which utilizes a layered graph structure derived from Wikipedia content combined with the YAHOO! Knowledge Graph. The proposed method leverages a multi-layered graph, constructed based on Wikipedia articles and their associated categorizations, to enhance entity recommendations. The underlying architecture of the Wikipedia website is used to compute a similarity metric among entities, which is then incorporated into a traditional recommendation framework to increase the accuracy of predictions. The YAHOO-WE system is implemented and successfully deployed as part of the Yahoo! Malaysia's innovative entity recommendation platform. Experimental evaluations using both offline and real-world online data demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, with YAHOO-WE achieving notable gains in recommendation performance and real-world adoption. Furthermore, the scalability and reliability of the YAHOO-WE system in production are highlighted, with the model's performance well-maintained across large dataset updates. The YAHOO-WE implementation is also open-sourced, providing a pioneering example for integrating Wikipedia content in Knowledge Graph-based entity recommendations. The entity recommendations produced by YAHOO-WE have been widely utilized across various Yahoo! Malaysia mobile applications and websites. The paper provides a comprehensive overview of the proposed approach, with a detailed discussion on the design choices, implementation, and both rigorous experimental evaluations and real-world deployments of the YAHOO-WE system. Moreover, the paper is concluded with a thoughtful examination of the potential applications and strengths of the YAHOO-WE architecture, as well as the potential areas for improvement and future research directions. We introduce a comprehensive and flexible $N$-body simulation technique that incorporates various cosmological theories with altered gravitational forces. This method is based on a modified gravitational potential function $f(\psi)$, where $\psi$ represents the standard gravitational potential field divided by its typical strength. The technique bypasses the need for a precise theory-based implementation, allowing it to seamlessly accommodate a broad spectrum of cosmological models. As a specific example, we adapt this method to simulate the effects of conformal coupling models, which involve modifying the gravitational constant in proportion to the cosmic energy density. The resulting $N$-body simulations retain the same computational efficiency as standard $\Lambda$CDM simulations, with each simulation consisting of approximately 500 CPU hours on 256 processors. We leverage this method to investigate the behavior of collisionless particles within a $\Lambda$CDM universe, spanning multiple large-scale structures and spanning physical scales from galaxy clusters to the cosmic web. The derived particle trajectories are accurate down to 10% at both the cluster and cosmic web scales, with an apparent shift in power law scaling from $m^{-0.18}$ to $m^{-0.26}$ as the mass of a cluster increases from $\sim 10^{14}$ to $\sim 10^{15}$ solar masses. Furthermore, we find that typical galaxy clusters exhibit 20-30% density deficiencies compared to $\Lambda$CDM predictions, with corresponding overestimations of their characteristic sizes, and we observe enhanced radial motion patterns within filaments, resulting in multiple bridging structures that connect clusters through vast distances. These findings hold significant implications for solving the cluster crisis, the hubble tension, and certain discrepancies in galaxy evolution phenomena. Additionally, we discover that a wide range of cosmological modifications, including those causing the matter-dominated era to shift or those altering the gravitational constant, can be simultaneously accommodated within this simulation framework. Furthermore, we explore potential observational signatures associated with modified gravity at both the galaxy and galaxy cluster scales, and we make available extensive simulation data, proxy models, and analysis tools on our website. Lastly, we outline several future directions for further investigation arising from these findings and the capabilities of this simulation technique. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. Contrary to this theory, researchers have studied the patterns of outbursts in another type of variable X-ray sources - those associated with neutron stars in binary systems. By examining the time spans between outbursts for these sources, researchers have attempted to validate or refute the idea that the absence of recent outbursts in some of these systems could be explained by a neutron star rather than a stellar mass black hole. Additionally, this approach can provide insights into the overall population of neutron star binaries observed at the Milky Way's center. Data from various outbursts observed by the all-sky monitor on board the Rossi X-ray satellite constellation, spanning from 1996 to 2016, were analyzed for a sample of 13 neutron star binaries exhibiting transient X-ray outbursts. By modeling the distribution of recurrence intervals between outbursts, researchers have estimated a population of 13 million neutron star binaries within the Milky Way. This estimate is significantly higher than previous models predicting the population of these binaries and raises concerns about the future visibility of these sources. Furthermore, none of the previously documented neutron star transient binaries in the Milky Way showed any outbursts during the 16-year observation period used for analysis. This implies that a substantial fraction of neutron star binaries in the Milky Way will not display outbursts visible with the all-sky monitor within a typical X-ray binary's recurrence time frame. As a result, identifying the nature of a variable X-ray source at the Milky Way's center solely on the basis of whether a source has shown an outburst during the 16 years of all-sky monitoring and none since then is incorrect and may be misleading. It is contended that a significantly lower visibility threshold is required to confidently claim the presence of a stellar mass black hole in the Milky Way's center. Systematic searches for outbursts triggered by real-time data analysis from the all-sky monitor and supported by follow-up observations with high-resolution telescopes are considered the most effective approaches for detecting a population of neutron star binaries and stellar mass black holes in the Milky Way's center. Additionally, deep X-ray observations using the next generation of X-ray telescopes such as the X-ray surveyor will be crucial in enhancing the detection of these variables and confirming the existence of a significant population of these compact binaries within the Milky Way's center

We demonstrate the significance of considering wavevector-dependent electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions, which are crucial in quantizing vibrations within crystalline structures. Using a linear response approach, we examine the impact on magnetic anisotropy and thermoelectric effects, showing that these phenomena are influenced by these dependencies. Furthermore, we indicate that large reductions in magnetic anisotropy lifetimes could be achieved through phonon engineering. Our analysis also reveals that the thermoelectric anomaly at the Fermi level can be modified by electron-phonon interactions. Additionally, we introduce a proposal for phonon-induced spin exchange interactions in type-I superconductors. Our theoretical framework is applicable to metals and superconductors, and we provide a method for calculating these interactions from first principles. We apply this framework to the case of phonon-induced spin exchange interactions in s-wave superconductors, demonstrating that these interactions can be repulsive or attractive, dependent on material parameters. We anticipate that our findings will contribute to a deeper comprehension of the phenomena arising from electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions in metals and superconductors. Nonetheless, the results presented here are specifically relevant to the materials barium titanate, strontium titanate, and copper oxide-based materials. Additionally, the paper concludes with an examination of some open questions in the field. Edited versions of the authors' individual introductory lectures on $\tau$-tilting theory, these notes cover a broad range of topics of interest to the field's leading researchers. Originally presented at the 2018 $\tau$-tilting theory workshop in Seoul, the material has since been revised and expanded in its printed form. Recent advances in conversational AI have been driven by large-scale dialog datasets crafted through crowdsourcing and industrial processes. Nonetheless, assessments and evaluations for these models have relied heavily on testing their ability to generate plausible next utterances in a conversation. We propose a novel evaluation framework that focuses on assessing the semantic richness and diversity of responses produced by models, leveraging Natural Language Inference (NLI) tasks to select diverse, semantically distinct labels as alternative responses. Through experiments involving the selection of richly varied response labels by NLI models, our findings highlight the limitations of current state-of-the-art models in generating semantically diverse dialogue responses. We further demonstrate that fine-tuning dialogue models on diverse targets yields superior results, surpassing baseline models built with generative training objectives. Our methodology and data are openly disseminated, enabling the creation of complex NLI tasks mirroring real-world conversational scenarios. Overall, our proposed framework offers a fresh perspective on evaluating the semantic aspects of conversational systems. The model's predictions align with existing data and theoretical frameworks, such as the 'fast-cook' model, and provide new insights that may be tested through future observations. Deep neural network approaches have achieved great success in various AI applications, yet their ability to adapt to continually changing datasets is limited. Incremental learning algorithms address this challenge by enabling models to incorporate new data without forgetting previously learned information. However, these algorithms struggle with learning from datasets that gradually shift and become unbalanced. Currently, there is a significant gap in research on imbalanced class incremental learning, with few algorithms available and no comprehensive evaluation existing to date. This paper contributes a thorough comparison of existing approaches, including both traditional methods and novel techniques, to explore ways to tackle this problem. We introduce a standard evaluation protocol, featuring six algorithms including three established methods, one proposed technique, and two variants of a base architecture. The results indicate that forgetting and bias have a significant impact on performance in this setting, with the base architecture consistently outperforming all other methods across different experiments. Furthermore, our research highlights the importance of directly addressing forgetting and data distribution shifts in future ICIIL algorithms. The code and data used in this comparison are made publicly available for the research community. Leveraging these results, we provide concrete directions for future work on novel architectures and loss functions to address the challenges of imbalanced class incremental learning. The findings and protocols presented in this study are applicable to various imbalanced datasets, beyond the ICIIL context. Despite the success of models in assessing the factual content of instructions, evaluating their procedural understanding is more complicated. To tackle this challenge, we introduce the concept of multimodal procedural knowledge, which involves sequencing disparate sections of instructional materials. To test this idea, we created the Multimodal Procedural Knowledge Sequencing (MPKS) Task, where participants must arrange unconnected paragraphs from various sources in a logical order, as indicated in sample books. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered at high frequencies by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for detecting gravitational waves produced by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by enhancing the quantum efficiency and signal-to-noise ratio, thereby improving the sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors at high frequencies. Using the LIGO A+ configuration as an example, we demonstrate that the sloshing Sagnac interferometer geometry can enhance the detector's sensitivity by 10-20% in the 500 Hz to 2 kHz frequency range. Furthermore, we find that this design is feasible with the current technology and resources allocated for the next-generation gravitational wave detectors. Furthermore, the sloshing Sagnac design can also enhance the sensitivity of intermediate-bandwidth detectors, such as those being developed for the Einstein Telescope, by a factor of 1.5 to 2 within the 500 Hz to 2 kHz frequency range. The associated improvements in source parameter estimation for binary neutron star mergers are also discussed. The potential of the sloshing Sagnac design to enhance the sensitivity of gravitational wave detectors makes it an attractive consideration for future detector configurations. The concept may also be applicable to other interferometric gravitational wave detectors and laser interferometers used in other fields such as particle physics and astronomy. The implementation of the sloshing Sagnac design, however, does introduce new control systems and photo-recoupling techniques, which need careful consideration and further development. The detailed analysis and numerical modeling used to optimize this design can be made available upon request. The theoretical foundations of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer have been incorporated into the current version of the SAMpy software, which is an open-source tool for computing the signal-recoded analysis matrix of interferometric gravitational wave detectors. The name of this software has been changed to I4PI to reflect its expanded capabilities in computing the full incident matrix for multi-cavity interferometers. The modified version of the software, along with its source code, has been made available on the GitHub platform for the benefit of the gravitational wave community. This difficult problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To tackle this issue, we propose a novel framework called SADRNet, which involves a self-aligned dual face regression framework within a two-stage 3D face alignment and reconstruction system. The model is designed to tackle both pose and occlusion challenges. During training, SADRNet is tasked with both aligning and regressing three-dimensional face coordinates as well as classifying occlusion levels and head pose orientations. To mitigate the complexity of modeling extensive pose data, we developed a head pose grouping scheme, which segments the possible solution space into more manageable subsets based on mid-face structure information. We also introduced an occlusion-aware loss function, along with a multi-task learning approach that facilitates robust learning across various real-world datasets through shared learning targets. The effectiveness of our proposed method is demonstrated through comprehensive evaluations on the widely used CelebA-B dataset and the more recently introduced Ianti-3DFACELR dataset. SADRNet achieves superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art techniques, particularly in scenarios with heavy occlusions and large head orientations. This study investigates the fundamental relationships between model performance, parameter count, and sample size for linear models with time series data and finds that these models exhibit benign overfitting on datasets obtained without data augmentation, particularly when powered by modern optimization methods and vast parameter spaces. Furthermore, our findings indicate that under such conditions, the estimated models possess a key ensembling property, where the optimal solution represents a combination of multiple local minima, resulting in a significant improvement in performance. We validate this theory through extensive simulations and examine the applications to real-world datasets, showcasing the benefits of linear models for time series data on multiple datasets. Additionally, we discover an intriguing applicability of two-problem linear regression, which facilitates approximate model performance and parameter understanding, before finally exploring effective regularization techniques in an unbiased manner. The implementation and results for the proposed methods are made available in the public repository https://github.com/zhengdengt/BOTSLM. The theoretical findings are also backed by the established generalization bounds, providing a framework for addressing future research questions, such as: How do structural assumptions on time series models influence their behavior on datasets? How do modern optimization methods compare to older alternatives in the context of over-parameterized models? The established generalization bounds also raise important questions about the behavior of models under miss-specification, the effects of different sampling schemes, and the underlying reasons for benign overfitting in linear models, which we hope this study will inspire future researchers to explore. Speech enhancement, a vital component in audio signal processing and the foundation for other advanced technologies like speech recognition and synthesis, is extensively researched. This paper showcases a novel deep learning architecture for speech enhancement. The proposed model, which is primarily based on the convolutional neural network framework, incorporates a groundbreaking attention mechanism within a bidirectional context. Within this attention mechanism, the model's complementary context is obtained from both the encoder and decoder components. This bidirectional context allows the model to focus in depth on the auditory signal's complex structure. Utilizing the proposed attention bidirectional multi-layer long short-term memory network, our model outperforms the existing state-of-the-art deep learning-based speech enhancement model. Experimental results indicate that our attention bidirectional structure delivers an overall 0.058 higher ssnr and 0.19 better si-snr compared to the existing state-of-the-art model. Furthermore, the proposed model exhibits superior subjective quality according to abr tests. The integrated attention bidirectional structure's effectiveness is demonstrated through additional modification flexibility, underscoring its potential as a versatile framework for speech modification tasks. A negative pressure room (NPR) in biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by using specialized systems to contain the microbes. Modern building management systems utilize differential pressure sensors (DPSs) to regulate and monitor NPR's air pressure. Our research reveals a non-intrusive vulnerability in these systems, where an attacker can induce resonance in DPSs using malicious audio at their natural frequencies, causing the sensors to malfunction. Our findings show that the resonant frequencies of most DPSs fall within the range of human hearing. We have demonstrated that we can design music capable of generating these resonant frequencies and, in doing so, trigger a significant discrepancy in pressure readings. Our research also shows that the malfunctions induced by this technique can fool the building management systems, potentially allowing pathogens to escape from NPRs. Our study highlights the urgency for further research into the resonant interactions between biological systems and sound, as well as the need for strengthened security protocols and the incorporation of sound-resistant materials in NPR construction. Our research has already inspired the development of a new sound-based attack on microphone arrays, which could further compromise NPR security. Our research team suggests that biologists, medical professionals, and everyone who works with or is exposed to infectious agents be aware of the risks associated with sound-induced pressure malfunctions and the precautions they can take to mitigate them. Our research also emphasizes the importance of sound study in biology, particularly in the areas of bioacoustics and symbiotic species. Furthermore, our research has sparked the development of an acoustic attack on microphone arrays, stress balls that induce resonant frequencies in DPSs, and calls for sound to be recognized as a legitimate physical quantity in biology. A key challenge in modeling decentralized energy markets involves capturing the behavior of self-sufficient players, who both produce and consume energy. To tackle this, we develop an expression for the maximum expected reward that these players can achieve, subject to given storage constraints. To do so, we transform the problem into a series of smaller stochastic optimization problems, and apply robust optimization techniques to account for uncertain demand. As a result, we obtain a risk-averse formulation that can be seen as minimizing the maximum regret experienced by the player, and can be solved using a variant of the Wasserstein distance. To demonstrate its practical utility, we apply the model to a sample market consisting of 120,000 households in Texas, simulating its behavior using a range of regression-based demand models. Notably, our approach yields results comparable to those of more complex methods, such as grid search, with a significant reduction in computational costs. Furthermore, the model exhibits storage substitution, where the use of storage leads to greater reward, and we observe multiple equilibrium solutions, including some with little to no storage, corresponding to different reward levels. Additionally, the model predicts an average storage size of around 1-2 kilowatt-hours per household, and can be used to design more effective storage policies. Finally, we find that our approach can handle a high level of demand uncertainty, and the resulting policies are robust across various weather conditions and seasonality. Moreover, the model can be used to investigate various market design, such as supply-side competition, and even extended to accommodate new technologies, such as electric vehicles, with suitable modifications. Finally, the model can be implemented using standard optimization libraries, such as CPLEX and GUROBI, and is suitable for large-scale applications, such as modeling the behavior of entire states. Additionally, the model can be used to design more effective storage policies, such as paying users for charging during periods of low demand, and can even be extended to address issues like voltage regulation. To do this, we divide the decision-making process into two stages, first determining the optimal charging and discharging strategy, and then using this self-allocation to meet the overall reward target. A combination of laser-driven spontaneous emission and the vacuum field of the cavity results in the formation of entangled states between two distant dipole locations. This entanglement, paired with the coherent response of the dipoles to a probing laser, allows for accurate measurement of the optical phase. Furthermore, we show that increasing the duration of the entanglement generation phase, or incorporating a squeeze operation, both enhance the precision of the phase measurement. These proposals can be executed with the current technological capabilities, and using long-lived dipoles offers the advantage of withstanding larger probing lasers. Consequently, this approach offers a superior phase measurement precision compared to other methods. Additionally, we indicate that employing a highly squeezed state may also yield optimal results. This novel method proposes the use of boson pair production, inspired by the principles of atomic physics, for determining optical phase. This novel approach outperforms existing methods, demonstrating that there is room for improving precision in optical phase measurement. Furthermore, we anticipate that implementing this method will contribute positively to the development of quantum technology. Moreover, we foresee applications of this method extending to other fields, such as quantum chemistry and quantum computing. Researchers who study donor-based quantum computing in silicon face a challenge: without precise experimental data, it's difficult to assess the accuracy of their theoretical models. Specifically, there's a lack of empirical evidence to support descriptions of valley and spin interactions for donors in silicon. To address this issue, our approach uses a variety of classical potential models to simulate the behavior of hydrogen-like donors in silicon, relying on hundreds of millions of simulations to build a comprehensive dataset of energy levels and probabilities. By analyzing these simulations through a lens of ci physics, the results can be accurately predicted with only a small number of parameters, making it possible to identify the most critical factors that influence these predictions. Furthermore, our method allows us to simulate exchange-coupled donors and demonstrate an alternative approach to modeling these systems, showcasing a notable agreement with existing theories. By applying our method to a range of scenarios, including the comparison of different classical potential models and the effect of lattice vibrations, we gain valuable insights that can inform future experimental and theoretical studies. Ultimately, our approach emphasizes the importance of rigorous simulation and a critical examination of theoretical models in the field of quantum computing. The underlying data and simulations used in this study have been made publicly available and can be utilized as a benchmark for evaluating classical potential models and donor simulations in silicon. The accompanying code is also available for further modification and integration into the development of donor-based quantum applications. The associated dataset has a total size of approximately 13GB and comprises over 1.5 billion rows of data, detailing the energy levels and probability distributions for donors in silicon. Our investigation focused on the conductance of a point contact made from HgTe quantum wells, which exhibit gapless behavior due to their unique Dirac fermion distribution. When a magnetic field is applied perpendicular to the charge carrier plane, the contact's conductance displays an intricate, hysteretic pattern. This complex behavior is severely impeded when the magnetic field surpasses a certain critical point, which is directly related to the carrier concentration, yet remains unaffected by the applied voltage. The conducting regime within the critical point is characterized by quasi-resonant conductance patterns resulting from the interaction between opposing spin subbands and involves the transmission of carriers through two vortex states. Furthermore, quasi-resonant conductance patterns emerge when the magnetic field is applied at an angle to the carrier plane, and their shape is determined by the angle itself. The study of these conductance patterns offers valuable insights into the investigation of zero-energy states in HgTe quantum wells. Additionally, quasi-resonant patterns may have applications in the development of sensitive magnetic field detectors. Despite intense research into the Hall anomaly of type-II superconductors, particularly in mixed-state transport, its underlying cause remains unclear. Vacancies in a pinned vortex lattice have been proposed as a possible explanation, but a quantitative analysis from this perspective is lacking in current literature. In this paper, we relate the Hall anomaly to a different response of the vortex lattice, specifically focusing on a proposed relationship between the lattice's shear resistance and vacancy density. Results from BSCCO thin-film samples, specifically those with high magnetic fields and low temperatures, are used to support this theory. These findings suggest that vacancies in the vortex lattice play a crucial role in determining the Hall signal. Furthermore, this proposed vacancy model offers a useful framework for understanding other transport phenomena observed in these materials. In addition, we investigate the dynamics of the vortex lattice by extracting the shear resistance at high magnetic fields, which reveals that the vacancy density can be tuned through adjustments to the applied pressure. The implications of these results on the broader understanding of vortex dynamics are also discussed in this paper. In particular, we examine how the vacancy density affects the lattice's thermal activation and relaxation mechanisms, proposing a revised phase diagram as a result of these findings. Consequently, the improved Hall effect measurements presented in this paper can provide valuable insights into the vacancy density of a material, potentially offering a non-local probe of the vacancy density within the vortex lattice. In conclusion, the quantitative analysis of the Hall effect in the vortex state, coupled with the proposed vacancy model, represents a significant step forward in the fundamental understanding of type-II superconductors. Additionally, we believe that the strategies employed in this study can be adapted to further investigate the physics of vortex matter in these materials. In the context of the broader field of superconductivity research, the results presented in this paper underscore the importance of experimental and theoretical advances in understanding the physics of vortex states. Researchers propose a new method to assess the critical behavior of systems at their phase transition points by calculating the second and higher-order moment correlations of the order parameter, which remains universally defined regardless of the system's underlying physics. Using this approach, we investigate the 3D Ising model using an Ising-Hamiltonian Monte Carlo simulation. Our findings reveal that in the equilibrated, critical state, the dimensionless moment correlations follow a power law with exponents dependent on the system size and spatial dimension. To overcome these size and dimensional constraints, we normalized the moment correlations by their values in small systems, thereby determining the universal scaling behavior of the 3D Ising universality class. Our results show that these normalized moments exhibit a logarithmic difference with exponents consistent across different orders, indicating a linear relationship with a common slope. This shared slope indicates that the logarithmic term can be expressed as a cumulative sum of independent, random variables, providing insight into the underlying dynamics that drive the behavior of systems in the 3D Ising universality class. Furthermore, our work paves the way for exploring other universality classes using this standardized approach. Additionally, we explore the possibility of quantifying the approach to equilibrium by analyzing the temporal evolution of these normalized moments, which exhibit distinct, system-size-dependent behaviors that influence the critical state in accordance with the 2D or 1D Ising universality classes. Our results have significant implications for conducting Monte Carlo simulations in lattice systems and reveal the importance of ensuring that systems have reached equilibrium before applying universal, order-parameter-based analyses. Our study demonstrates that such tests are necessary, especially when interpreting simulations based on magnetic susceptibility, which can be influenced by irreversible components and may not always serve as a reliable indicator of equilibrium or a system's critical behavior. Our findings are further validated using numerical solution methods for the Ising model's equation of state, which reveals that even for large systems, the logarithmic term can be understood through its individual, random variables, confirming the effectiveness of our normalized moment approach. A characterization of finite-dimensional commuting squares for subfactors of finite depth is provided, based on the theory of higher representation symmetry. Additionally, the characterization involves the invariant of the square, represented by a matrix product operator in a longosemigroups, and satisfies the Haagerup approximation property. Notably, this characterization serves as a precursor to higher representation fusion rules. Our research also reveals that higher representation symmetry endows subfactors with properties similar to those of conformal quantum field theories. Moreover, we establish that the duality of higher representation symmetry holds, implying that the central charge of a subfactor is non-negative. Our findings rely on the theory of higher category symmetry constructed through the work of Kawahigashi and Longo, and on the approximation properties of subfactors. Our characterizations of commuting squares for subfactors of finite depth contribute to the broader understanding of these structures. Furthermore, our research is complementary to the recent findings of Ng, but independently reaches the conclusion that the Haagerup approximation property is a crucial aspect of such squares. Our results also highlight the significance of higher category symmetry in the study of subfactors, and demonstrate how this symmetry gives rise to numerous properties of these structures. Recent neural network models, such as Hamiltonian Neural Networks, have generated significant interest in the physics and mathematics communities by potentially offering an physically inspired and mathematically grounded framework for data modeling.  One crucial aspect to understand the capabilities of these models is the analysis of their learned representations, which is the main focus of our investigation.  We critically examine the ability of HNNs to learn derivatives of functions by analyzing their latent representation and verifying our findings with concrete experiments.  Our results indicate that HNNs learn the latent variables corresponding to function derivatives rather than the actual derivatives themselves.  As a remedy, we propose an enhanced version of HNNs called the Hamiltonian Derivative Neural Network (HDNN) that learns the required derivatives in addition to the original function.  Our HDNN model achieves remarkable performance on real-world benchmark datasets for function prediction, surpassing the performance of conventional models like Hamiltonian Neural Networks and baseline models like Physics-informed Neural Networks and Continuous-time Neural Networks.  Furthermore, we find that both the normal HNN and our proposed HDNN model have the capability to successfully tackle inverse problems, notably we find that both of these models are capable of reconstructing functions and their derivatives from limited pointwise measurements, a capability that is heavily dependent on the architecture's ability to capture the Koopman operator's eigenfunctions, providing a groundbreaking insight into the behavior of continuous-time neural networks. As deep learning models interact with humans in various roles such as voice assistants and virtual assistants, ensuring their reliability and consistency is crucial. We propose an innovative multi-agent system to address this concern. Initially, a machine learning model generates predictions and calculates a confidence score for each, while a reinforcement learning-based agent, influenced by these confidence levels, selects training data for optimization. Meanwhile, a natural language processing agent crafts human-friendly statements to inform the user of the model's progress and proposed adjustments. When the model's inaccuracies exceed a certain threshold, it is deemed untrustworthy, and the user is notified. In response, the user designates specific categories of data as reliable or un reliable, which influences the model's training and boosts its performance. In addition, the user has the option to increase the diversity of data used for training. Results from a virtual reality game demonstrate the effectiveness of this system in enhancing the model's accuracy and overall trustworthiness. Code is available on GitHub. With the proposed approach, we believe it is possible to achieve a higher level of trust in deep learning models through a collaborative human-in-the-loop process. Furthermore, the proposed multi-agent system can be applied across various domains as a solution to the data reliability problem. The name of the system, "Joint Trust Building," reflects its underlying principle of simultaneously building human trust and model performance. With the increasing presence of artificial intelligence in everyday life, validating the accuracy and reliability of these models will become essential. We anticipate future research directions to focus on scaling the system, integrating explanations into the modeling process, and exploring alternative human-AI collaboration frameworks. The proposed system has inherent flaws, which future research aims to rectify. Consequently, enhancing the robustness, efficiency, and generalizability of the model will be essential considerations for future implementations. The need for human input and the subjectivity inherent in human decisions may raise concerns about the model's generalizability and potential for biased outcomes. Nonetheless, the proposed approach offers a pioneering human-AI collaboration framework that can be applied across various domains and potentially becomes a standard method for modeling real-world domains. The time spent by the human partner on providing feedback and making decisions may seem considerable; however, it is essential to control the model's trusted zone and ensure safe human-AI collaboration. The performance of the model may decline when compared to models trained using the standard stochastic gradient descent method; however, this drawback is offset by the increase in the model's trustworthiness. The model's trustworthiness is a key factor in its successful deployment

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies employing contextual information to enhance BERT's existing capabilities.  However, the existing literature largely overlooks the significance of glosses, which comprise definitions or descriptions associated with each word sense.  By integrating this contextual information, we hypothesize that WSD performance can be further optimized.  To test this hypothesis, we propose a context-gloss enhancement model, incorporating both contextual and gloss-related information to fine-tune the pre-trained language model BERT.  The evaluation of our model across three diverse datasets highlights the importance of using glosses and the effectiveness of the proposed architecture in enhancing the disambiguation of word senses.  The enhanced performance achieved through the context-gloss model serves as a basis for exploring the integration of semantic networks within the attention mechanism of transformer models.  Our work contributes to the exploration of glosses as contextual information in the embedding-based WSD framework.  The strong relationship between the definition of a word sense and its context suggests that the employment of glosses can augment the existing methods using a multi-sense embedding-based WSD approach.  The proposed framework also offers a novel design for modeling word sense ambiguity within a multi-sense embedding framework, providing an alternative to the currently prevalent composition-based methods.  The enhanced performance achieved through the context-gloss enhancement model has significant implications for the development of sophisticated linguistic models, capable of processing text with multiple word sense ambiguities.  The significant role of glosses in the proposed model raises important considerations for the selection of semantic networks and the implementation of the transformer model.  The context-gloss enhancement model serves as a pioneering example for incorporating the abundance of available word sense definitions or descriptions, embedded within the knowledge base, into the attention mechanism of transformer models.  The model's performance provides a benchmark for future studies seeking to further explore the utilization of glosses and the investigation of various implementations of the transformer model.  The data used in this study are publicly available, providing valuable insights for the development of future word sense disambiguation systems.  The findings of this research can be applied across multiple domains, enabling the construction of more accurate and reliable models for real-world applications. We investigate a particular application, where the goal is to generate structured queries based on natural language prompts. To illustrate the challenge of this task, we utilize SPAD-GOLD, a comprehensive dataset spanning nine popular datasets. Notably, SPAD-GOLD encompasses not just datasets over real-world databases, but also features an extensive set of evaluation metrics tailored to assess the complete end-to-end text-to-SQL pipeline. We emphasize the necessity of developing a robust understanding of language through these structured queries and showcase a pioneering cross-domain approach. This approach divides the pipeline into two separate understanding tasks: first converting natural language prompts into a intermediate representation, and subsequently using this representation to generate structured queries. We introduce a novel dual encoder model addressing both of these tasks simultaneously, but also explore a more straightforward alternative that models each task individually. This alternative was particularly effective on SPAD-GOLD, achieving a significant boost in performance. We further highlight the benefits of evaluating the language understanding ability of models like BART through text-to-SQL tasks and showcase a way to adapt these models to new databases and domains.
