In this research, we propose a method to automatically generate complex road networks for testing the limits of autonomous lane-keeping technology in simulation. By using a set of control points to define the path, we create a simulated environment with real-world characteristics, complete with markers and signs, to evaluate the system's performance. To assess the system's ability to handle continuous challenges, we introduce a "survival period" as a measure of the system's stability, and through simulations, we validate the effectiveness of our approach in producing challenging scenarios. Additionally, we demonstrate the feasibility of incorporating real-world data into the system, enabling the generation of more realistic and diverse scenarios. Further, we explore ways to enhance the created scenarios through optimization techniques, leading to further improvement in the field. The proposed method facilitates the creation of high-quality test cases, accelerating the development and enhancement of lane-keeping systems. The implementation, utilizing C++ and OpenALKS, facilitates integration with system simulations, allowing for a more comprehensive testing environment. The developed method is adaptable to various road types and conditions, making it a versatile solution. Overall, this research provides a groundbreaking approach to creating robust road networks for testing autonomous lane-keeping systems, paving the way for more efficient and effective development processes. The proposed method has far-reaching implications, influencing the evolution of lane-keeping systems and paving the path for its application in various mobility scenarios. Additionally, the approach has been made available on the OpenALKS repository, enabling widespread adoption. Further, we have explored incorporating machine learning into the proposed method, leading to a possible integration of optimized scenarios. However, this investigation remains ongoing. Overall, this research has provided a groundbreaking solution, addressing the significant challenge of developing robust test cases for the next generation of lane-keeping systems. The implementation has facilitated a deeper understanding of the subject matter, obtained through participation in the IROS 2021 conference. Lastly, we have established collaborations with leading technology companies, propelling the development of lane-keeping systems forward. Nonetheless, numerous questions still linger, such as "What are the open-ended questions derived from this discussion?" and "How might we further solidify these findings through additional experiments?".

Temporal action detection is focused on pinpointing the exact start and end times of actions within a video. A key challenge lies in existing boundary matching methods that exhaustively evaluate all possible combinations of start and end times but fail to capture the long-term context. Moreover, densely generated proposals with adjacent semantics do not improve semantic uniqueness. To address this issue, we present a new approach called Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN) for producing high-quality action proposals through end-to-end proposal generation, where we incorporate contextual information at both action boundary and proposal levels. For action boundary detection, we employ Multi-Path Temporal Context Aggregation (MTCA) for context aggregation and accurate boundary assessment, while Coarse-to-fine Matching (CFM) is used for context aggregation and matching refinement at the proposal level. Our method has achieved exceptional performance on ActivityNet v1.3 and THUMOS-14, achieving an average mean average precision (mAP) of 35.39% and 54.14% mean average precision at intersection over union 0.5 respectively, solidifying DCAN as a top-performing method. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a stress increase that mirrors the initial surge. Despite its frequent occurrence in both natural and man-made environments, the shear thickening transition (STT) phenomenon remains poorly understood at a fundamental level. Our research involves actively probing viscoelastic materials both below and above the STT using dynamic mechanical spectroscopy, which allows us to examine the underlying elasticity in each regime. By analyzing our data using a proven theory for entangled polymers and using our results to establish a stress-based relationship, we demonstrate that the shear thickening transition forms an orderly sequence of interconnected states that can be mapped onto a single global curve when plotted against stress. This finding provides a clear framework for understanding the complex behavior observed during STTs and lays the groundwork for a universal theory of these events. This research paper proposes a novel approach to developing safety-critical controllers for complex control systems subject to input limitations. Specifically, it outlines the development of an Input Constrained Control Barrier Function, which pinpoints a secure subset of possible system states and designs a control mechanism to maintain those states. The devised controller can be optimized through an efficiently solvable quadratic program, enabling real-time application. Building upon earlier concepts of Higher Order Control Barrier Functions, ICCBFs demonstrate the ability to tackle a broader class of nonlinear systems, including those that can exhibit chaotic behavior, and showcase their effectiveness through simulation examples. Finally, the paper highlights potential extensions and applications for ICCBFs. 

The paper further introduces a formal language to express input constraints within Control Barrier Function frameworks, specifically targeting Higher Order Control Barrier Functions. This proposed syntax, based on Linear Temporal Logic, can capture a wide range of constraint patterns, and is accompanied by an accompanying tool that can automatically convert these specifications into executable code suitable for real-time control systems. This conversion process involves a novel algorithm that converts LTL formulas into efficient Higher Order Control Barrier Function configurations, and is showcased through examples in the associated document. 

The second part of the paper extends the input constrained control barrier function framework to accommodate dynamic system observations, leading to the concept of a Control Barrier Function for an estimated system. It then demonstrates the ability to solve optimization problems subject to estimated system security constraints, until which point the solution remains feasible with respect to the true system. Furthermore, it explores potential applications and future research directions for this concept, and provides numerical examples illustrating its effectiveness. 

The third part of the paper explores novel control synthesis methods, centered on reformulating dynamic feedback control problems as boundary value problems, and subsequently solving resulting ordinary and partial differential equations. It then demonstrates the ability to solve complex dynamic feedback optimization problems subject to security constraints, and presents accompanying simulation examples.

This study introduces the concept of CF-approximation spaces, which can represent diverse geographic areas using a limited set of point locations. These locations, or features, may correspond to coordinates of location points, attribute values at grid cells, or data values at measurement sites. We demonstrate that any geographic area can be precisely mirrored by creating a CF-approximation space with an appropriate set of feature functions. Furthermore, we show that both vector representations and tessellations can be accurately captured with CF-approximation spaces. Additionally, we outline effective methods for computing and comparing these spaces, which can be used for comparative analyses of geographic areas. These comparisons can be used to determine the similarity or differences between locations, which has practical applications in, for example, identifying location changes over time. These concepts and methods can also be applied to data aggregation, where the characteristics of geographic areas can be determined from the features within those areas. These ideas have been implemented in the open-source Python library geopdisso. This library is an advanced spatial analysis toolkit that provides sophisticated location comparison and aggregation capabilities, surpassing the capabilities of commonly used geographic information systems. This research is an extension of previous work on the cf-space framework and the geographical description language, and both an interactive visualization tool and an implementation in R are also available.

We define loom areas as a broader class of polygons that contain the loom of a mapping class group action, and demonstrate that these polygons determine a veering triangulation. Furthermore, we establish that the boundary of a loom area is a nondegenerate stratum of the veering fiber space, and that the pattern of these strata is dictated by the fiber pattern of the veering triangulation. Additionally, we show that the loom area can be used to model a specific sequence of fiber space crossings, and with this in mind, we introduce the concept of chronologically ordered strata. We then prove that any veering triangulation can be constructed from a sequence of loom areas that are in a specific order, known as the chronological order, which defines a particular ordering of the strata of the veering fiber space. We also establish that this order is broader than the order implied by the flow of the action that gives rise to the veering triangulation. We further explore the properties of this order, and demonstrate that it gives rise to a order on the collection of boundaries of loom areas, which forms a poset. We also prove that this poset has a natural representation as a order on the collection of boundaries of smoothly embedded minimal surfaces in the unit 3-ball, and that it is equivalent to the order defined by inclusion. We also show that the poset has a key property known as the strong exchange property, and that this property is responsible for the increased complexity of some of the elements in the poset as compared to their counterparts in the corresponding category of surfaces. We also prove that any order defined by a system of interacting particles that satisfy a specific property, known as the SIEP, can be represented as the order on the collection of boundaries of loom areas, and that this order has the strong exchange property. We also discuss the implications of this result for the theory of the SIEP, and we also prove that the order on the collection of boundaries of loom areas can be defined by a system of interacting particles that satisfy a specific property, known as the SIEP, and that this system can be realized in the unit 3-ball. We also prove that the order on the collection of boundaries of loom areas is a robust feature that can be seen in different levels of description, and that it gives rise to a property known as the property of increasing complexity, and that this property can be seen in both the abstract, abstract-approximate, and exact levels. These models combine node features with the graph structure, creating flexible and effective models, but they can be challenging to interpret due to their implicit representation of node interactions and graph connectivity. To address this issue, we developed a novel approach called PRUN, which systematically reduces graph neural network complexity for both interpretation and performance improvement. By successively eliminating sensitive edges based on their contribution to model predictions, PRUN creates a simplified subgraph that mimics the original model's classification capabilities. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PRUN through efficient sparsification of numerous graph neural network architectures, resulting in significant reductions in model size (averaging 70% percent of original parameters) and a notable improvement in accuracy (averaging 3.5% percent increase) across real-world benchmark datasets. Furthermore, PRUN's output provides a clear, data-driven explanation for classification decisions. To facilitate further research, we also introduce the concept of learned sparsification and corresponding evaluation metrics, along with an open-source code repository for reproducibility and customization. Our approach is applicable to a broad range of GNN models and can be adapted for various sparsification strategies, offering a versatile framework for the interpretation and improvement of graph neural networks. By integrating PRUN with model training, we also introduce an alternative strategy called antecedent-based sparsification, which leverages historical sparsification results to inform future model training in an efficient and data-driven manner. This method allows for the development of more complex models that yield superior performance on external test datasets. Comprehensive experiments showcase the efficacy of both PRUN and its variant, highlighting their potential to enhance model interpretability, performance, and generalizability. This deformation preserves features like Ahlfors regularity, Poincare inequality validity, and tangent cones with positive scalar curvature. In Part II, we employ surgery-style arguments to successfully remove the singular sets, following similar principles used to eliminate the singular sets found in Euclidean space. Ultimately, this leads to the achievement of our initial goal of demonstrating that manifolds with positive scalar curvature and a compact, singular set have a minimal, related geometry that can be deformed. Consequently, this implies the existence of a family of conformally equivalent manifolds sharing key characteristics with the original manifold. In particular, this results in the elimination of the original manifold's singular sets, further confirming a related conjecture originally proposed by G. Tian and S. Zhang. A heat-driven motion of vortices in superconductors is influenced by a viscous force that impairs their circulation. To understand this phenomenon, researchers propose a new model that incorporates a heat-driven force and suggests that vortex motion generates two types of entropy: one that remains stationary and one that moves with the vortex flow. Conversely, this framework implies that entropy associated with the stationary part of the superfluid can influence the vortex liquid's viscosity. This theoretical model predicts an increase in the vortex liquid's entropy and a reduction in the predicted peak viscosity when compared to its normally high value. Using observations from KCWI and NOEMA, we studied a distant starburst galaxy, identifying a massive gas outflow originating from a specific star-forming ring within the galaxy. Our data show that the outflow is composed of two distinct components with differing velocities and chemical compositions, suggesting they interact with the host galaxy's dark matter halo. We discovered a significant relationship between the outflow's mass and star formation rates across the ring, along with enhanced activity in the center. Our results indicate that global outflows are controlled locally within the disk. Furthermore, we found that gas flows within the ring are bar-like and likely driven by the galaxy's rotational bar, and that the outflow's origin is tied to gas accumulations at the inner edge of the ring. Our study provides spatially resolved evidence of how global outflows are regulated by star formation within a galaxy's disk.

Current methods for creating simulations rely heavily on human-provided information, limiting their scalability and comprehensive coverage of real-world scenarios. To address this challenge, our proposed SceneGen model uses a novel approach to combine semantic maps with simple geometric forms, generating diverse and detailed traffic scenes through sequential construction. By training SceneGen on actual scenes, we've observed it can accurately model scene components and their relationships, resulting in statistically similar scene characteristics to those of the training data. The model's performance is assessed across multiple evaluation metrics for realistic scene generation. Furthermore, SceneGen demonstrates efficiency and practical application potential when integrated with leading scene construction methods. The model's code and documentation are available online. Additionally, we've established a public database containing hundreds of realistic traffic scenes, tailored for further model evaluations and testing. These scenes, unlike those created through human-based approaches, are cost-effective to produce and maintain. The metrics used for evaluating SceneGen's performance are also introduced as a set of quantitative standards for assessing the realism of generated scenes. The proposed SceneGen model provides an innovative solution for creating realistic traffic scenes through an automated process, paving the way for more effective simulation-based approaches in the development of autonomous vehicles. A combined ergodicity property for sequences of integers is introduced, based on the concept of van der Corput's difference theorem. It is demonstrated that this property has significant implications for the distribution of these sequences, enabling the derivation of robust ergodicity results. Specifically, we prove that two families of sequences, characterized by the presence of certain difference patterns and approximant sets, exhibit combined ergodicity. As a consequence, we show that sequences defined by recursive formulas exhibiting combined ergodicity can be used to generate values with distinct difference patterns, thereby yielding lower bounds on the measure of ergodic measures with full Lebesgue support. This approach bypasses the requirement for non-conjugacy among the sequences' underlying subsequences, expanding the scope of sequences covered by combined ergodicity. Finally, we outline a related conjecture related to Gowers' problem on ergodicity. While we establish that this conjecture holds for sequences defined by recursive formulas, we also identify a significant caveat. Additionally, we explore links between combined ergodicity and other distribution-related properties, including what can be described as almost combined ergodicity, almost joint ergodicity, and a combined version of the former, along with associated measures of ergodicity. These results, centered on sequences defined by recursive formulas, provide a unifying framework for previous works of Peluse and Prendiville, as well as of Peluse, Prendiville, and Smart. Furthermore, they establish a common foundation for three main subfields: almost combined ergodicity, almost joint ergodicity, and combined ergodicity; clarify the precise relationship between these properties; and highlight the pivotal role of difference patterns in the distribution of sequence-related phenomena. Finally, we investigate potential applications of combined ergodicity to Diophantine approximation and obtain related results on the prevalence of sequences with specific difference patterns among the forms of polynomial curves. These results, in turn, raise questions regarding the distribution of such difference patterns. Lastly, we outline key open questions and propose new conjectures arising from the results presented in this article. Detecting and classifying three-dimensional objects at great distances, or far-field detecion, presents a significant challenge for deep learning algorithms. Our investigation reveals that existing models excel at closer ranges but fall short when confronted with far-field targets. Furthermore, we find that ranking accuracy among targets decreases as the distance gap widens. To address this, we introduce a novel evaluation metric called the far-field mean average precision, or ffMAP, tailored to far-field detection scenarios. With ffMAP in mind, we present Far3Det, a far-field three-dimensional identification model, showcasing substantial performance enhancements over baseline methods across multiple datasets. Our findings suggest that targeted architectures, such as Far3Det, are essential for achieving superior ffMAP results. The Far3Det model and ffMAP metric are released alongside our research papers and code are available at https://github.com/linge wang/Far3Det. and will be presented at CVPR 2023. Additionally, we are launching the Far-Field 3D Object Detection Benchmark at https://linge-wang.github.io/Far3Det-Benchmark/. The Far-Field 3D Object Detection Benchmark aims to provide a comprehensive evaluation platform and venue for far-field three-dimensional object detection research. It will be hosted on the Detectron2 framework and supported by the Computer Vision Foundation. The Far-Field 3D Object Detection Benchmark is an open call for submissions, with plans to launch version 2.0 at ICLR 2024 and to hold a competition track at CVPR 2024. Full papers on our Far3Det approach have been accepted to CVPR 2023 and ICLR 2024, and a workshop related to far-field object detection will be organized at CVPR 2024 under the direction of Prof. Ling Wang. Leveraging large datasets, we present Far3Det-Shadow, a shadow-based detector that address the blind spot issue common in multi-view object detection. Our investigation indicates that targets with overlapping bounding boxes significantly impede the performance of detection algorithms. To tackle this challenge, we introduce Far3Det-Dual, a dual-type framework that tackles both near-field and far-field detection scenarios. Moreover, we launch the Far-Field 3D Object Detection in the Wild (FF3DOW) benchmark, along with Far3Det-Dual winning the competition at the CVPR 2023 benchmark competition. Additionally, we present Far3Det-Single, a real-time far-field detector achieving 54.4% ffMAP at 30 frames

In the development of realistic condensed matter systems using quantum computing, it is not practical to perform an exact diagonalization of large Hamiltonians for the calculation of ground states and physical properties. This study introduces a data-driven approach based on quantum machine learning, which generates approximate ground states for solid-state systems through an overcomplete set of trial states. The quality of the ground states is ensured by applying a diagonal ensemble based on the Hamiltonian and the trial states, and is indicated by the overlap with the true ground state. This methodology is applied to numerical simulations of spinless particles in one-dimensional harmonic potentials and in Su-Schrieffer-Heeger models, which demonstrate the ability to produce high-quality ground states with minimal data. The results show an exponential improvement in the overlap when increasing the number of data points used, and suggest that this approach can significantly reduce the amount of quantum information required for such calculations. The proposed framework is efficient, flexible, and suitable for integration with quantum simulation platforms that allow real-time monitoring of system parameters. The implementation of this protocol in quantum circuits is also outlined, along with the associated costs in gate count and depth. The results presented in this study demonstrate the potential of applying quantum machine learning to simulate complex condensed matter systems. The Su-Schrieffer-Heeger models used here are notable for their rich physics, including the explicit breaking of time-space symmetry and the tendency of systems to fragment when particle filling exceeds a certain threshold. The proposed algorithm is currently being explored for applications to lattice gauge theories and chemical reaction dynamics. The associated code is publicly available upon request. The study of systems like the ones examined here is expected to contribute to the broad understanding of quantum physics in solid-state systems. The results shown here are the outcome of a single-round simulation, and the protocol could be executed on the quantum platforms provided by the IBMQ, a QubitPair on the IBMQ Santiago, or a linear array of eight qubits on the IBMQ Toronto. The implementation of this protocol in quantum circuits involves the application of a diagonal ensemble based on the Hamiltonian and the trial states, and relies on the overlap with the true ground state to ensure the quality of the ground states. Soft-tissue procedures like liver and heart surgery are complicated by the uncertainty of organ structures before surgery. To address this challenge, doctors use respiratory and cardiovascular MRI scans to enhance surgical visibility. However, aligning pre-surgery maps with real-time surgery scans is a complex problem due to organ deformation. Existing methods primarily rely on surface registrations but struggle with significant non-rigid transformations. We propose a novel, semi-supervised approach that combines alignment and estimation tasks to facilitate non-rigid transformations. Initially, we build a multi-dimensional regression model to forecast alignment directions based on comparison maps, indicating how training data should be aligned. Next, we utilize this model to guide optimization, gradually refining the alignment until it converges with the regression predictions. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in accurately aligning complex organs with large non-rigid transformations, outperforming existing surface registration methods. Moreover, our approach requires substantially fewer training samples than traditional methods. We test our method on liver and heart data with substantial rigid and non-rigid transformations. Results show our approach produces more accurate alignments than conventional methods and even outperforms models specifically designed for non-rigid registrations, particularly in scenarios with significant rigid transformations. Furthermore, our approach boasts an order of magnitude more training flexibility. We facilitate the integration of our approach into the AlgoSurfer library, allowing easy integration with other algorithms. We also make our model's code available at https://github.com/CMU-ARI/NonRigidV2S. We explore the potential of modeling real-time surgery surfaces using volumetric representations and demonstrated models. However, further research is necessary to fully capture these temporal dynamics. We anticipate our approach to be applicable in video processing and other fields involving time-series data. In the context of surgery, enhancing surgical tools with more accurate and sensitive technology is also a promising direction. We expect this to interest researchers in the surgery and medicine communities and highlight the value of accurate data visualization. Additionally, we examine the possibility of extending our model to handle multiple organs and provide insights on potential areas of improvement and optimization. We conclude by highlighting the challenges and opportunities presented by the complexity of surgery procedures that involve structure uncertainty and the scope it has in other fields. Furthermore, we outline the scope and potential applications for our approach in data processing and surface estimation. Lastly, we provide a roadmap for further research on this issue and the implications it has for other data processing challenges. For autonomous driving applications, accurate scene flow estimation is crucial, as it calculates the motion of each pixel and provides a 3D disparity field. Unlike traditional methods that rely on supervised training, our proposed method achieves high-quality results without annotated training data. By transforming the training process into an adversarial game, our model learns to distinguish between metric disparities and non-disparities, with the help of two components: a flow model that generates pseudo annotations and a metric learner that refines the model's predictions based on these annotations. Through self-supervised learning, our model is able to prioritize motion information, ignore stationary objects, and reduce the impact of noisy counterparts. As a result, our model performs exceptionally well on the Cityscanes Hofegg dataset, achieving a 3.35% reduction in RMSE and outperforming state-of-the-art self-supervised scene flow estimation models. Moreover, our model exhibits robust performance on real-world datasets, surpassing canonical baseline models. Our code and model are publicly available for access. Furthermore, our model's ability to perform well without relying on external datasets makes it particularly useful for large-scale scene flow estimation applications. Through the integration of a static object detector, our model's effectiveness can be further enhanced by removing the impact of incorrectly classified stationary objects. Our model's performance in challenging scenarios is also enhanced by the inclusion of a quality metric, enabling the selection of high-quality training samples and resulting in a 6.12% RMSE reduction. As the proposed framework's architecture is flexible and modular, we explore the effects of model modifications on performance, leading to the integration of a multi-resolution flow model. This enables the model to prioritize coarse-motion information, leading to a 5.46% RMSE reduction. As a result, our model ranks first in self-supervised scene flow estimation benchmarks, outperforming canonical baseline models by a significant margin. Moreover, our model's performance is robust across real-world datasets, showcasing its potential as a leading solution for scene flow estimation challenges. We have presented the results from the AstroSat analysis of the high-mass X-ray binary X-ray pulsar IGR J19294+1816 during its Type-I outburst in October 2019. Timing and spectral data from the decline phase of the outburst revealed the spin period to be 12.485 seconds, with significant spectral features. A Quasi Periodic Oscillation was observed at a frequency of 0.032 Hz and an RMS amplitude of 18%. Our joint spectral analysis detected Cyclotron Resonant Scattering and Iron emission lines at 14.06 keV and 6.4 keV respectively, with no significant contribution from an inner accretion disk. These findings confirm the previous CRTS classification of IGR J19294+1816 as a long-duration transient and a persistent source, and also add the first QPO detection in the 2019 outburst, further highlighting the need for further research into this intriguing phenomenon. Moreover, the absence of a significant inner accretion disk during the decline of this outburst, along with the unique 2019 FASTeRT/FAST data, raises important considerations for the application of the Multijoint Technique used in this analysis.

Deep learning methods for LiDAR data analysis have revolutionized 3D place recognition in autonomous vehicles and robotics by improving local re-localization and loop-closure detection rates in complex environments. However, extracting robust, orientation-insensitive 3D descriptors from LiDAR data remains a persistent challenge. To tackle this, we introduce AttDLNet, an innovative model that leverages attention mechanisms to selectively emphasize contextual and inter-feature connections within a multi-layer perceptron, enabling efficient orientation-insensitive 3D descriptors. To optimize performance, we've developed a training framework that utilizes synthetic data and real-world supervisory cues. Our experiments demonstrate AttDLNet's capability to create highly accurate, robust, and orientation-insensitive place descriptors, outperforming existing state-of-the-art approaches like DLDH, PHGD, and FRNet across various evaluation metrics. Furthermore, we've found that our model excels in challenging scenarios, particularly in loops and long-distance place recognition tasks. Our code and associated resources are available online at https://github.com/hzhang88/AttDLNet. Our findings suggest that attention-based deep learning models can create exceptionally robust and efficient 3D place descriptors from LiDAR data, paving the way for their use in real-world robotic applications. Additionally, we've investigated the implications of loop-closure strategies on place recognition and presented a comprehensive analysis of loop-closure policies and associated challenges. Our research highlights the significance of supervisory-driven training methods in deep learning approaches for 3D place recognition. Finally, we've examined the scope for further exploration in the 3D place recognition domain. Our study's findings are relevant to both robotic navigation experts and researchers, and we've provided a detailed evaluation of AttDLNet's performance in real-world scenarios, including results from robust loop-closure tests and comparisons with all major recent deep learning-based 3D place recognition models. Speech imitation, the generation of new speech based on existing samples, has reached high accuracy in recent years. However, current methods focus primarily on visual guidance and ignore the potential benefits of auditory context. To address this limitation, we introduce MaskedSpeech, a novel task that utilizes auditory context to produce high-quality speech. In a benchmark testing scenario, MaskedSpeech performance falls just 0.02% behind unmasked speech production benchmarks. To facilitate training for this task, we also develop a scoring system and a modeling framework called Context-aware Speech Production with Masking Strategy, which involves unmasking speech samples based on auditory context. Our findings demonstrate the efficacy of our approach and model, and we openly share our dataset, evaluation metrics, and code to enable further advancements in this area. Additionally, we invite the community to participate in ongoing MaskedSpeech challenges through our open-source repository. Our research and model are relevant to applications such as speech-based acting and entertainment, where the auditory context can be leveraged to produce a more realistic and context-aware performance. Furthermore, we believe MaskedSpeech has the potential to enhance video-audio synthesis tasks that involve speech production. Our dataset and evaluation metrics can also be used to assess the contextual speech production abilities of other modeling frameworks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghulghulew/Context_speech_production and the dataset can be accessed at https://www.dropbox.com/s/cl2b1q5z1z1i4qf/Masked_speech_dataset.7z?dl=0. Large model implementations for evaluation purposes can be found at https://github.com/ghulghulew/Context_speech_production/tree/main/models. Our research is also discussed in the paper available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.03078. Our team participated in the LTA 2022 challenge and presented our work at the 2022 ICASSP conference practice session. Additionally, we have an ongoing project related to this task called MultiModSynthesis, which involves the simultaneous production of multiple modalities such as speech, video, and text, and can be explored through our open-source code https://github.com/ghulghulew/Multimodal-speech-production.... In a typical case, van Hove singularities in pseudogapped metals are not significantly affected by interactions with other particles. However, we have found an extraordinary instance where the singularities are intensified by electron-electron interactions, leading to pronounced features in specific energy regions. These intensified singularities may contribute to the varied rates at which different parts of the Fermi surface lose their energy content and participate in electrical conduction. This disparity can also be responsible for the difference between conduction velocities measured in different directions. These accelerated electrical transmissions might be harnched and propagate over extended distances, potentially giving rise to new types of phase transitions and other phenomena. Additionally, we have observed that the intense singularities can trigger the spontaneous breakdown of time-reversal symmetry. Furthermore, our theoretical predictions based on electron-electron interactions may be verified through experimental measurement of spectral functions using angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. These extra singularities can arise in metals with broken symmetry or near phase transitions, particularly in cases with time-reversal symmetry. A specific example is presented in an illustration of a specific material, Ba(Fe$_{0.925}$Mn$_{0.075}$)O$3-\delta$, where the extraordinary singularities may contribute to the emergence of the experimentalized spin-triplet superconductivity. These extra singularities can also give rise to the observed phenomena of electron nematicity and may be responsible for the non-quadratic term in the expansion of the self-energy in energy. These findings are further substantiated by additional measurements that may provide further insight into the underlying processes giving rise to the observed phenomena. These predictions raise the possibility that time-reversal-breaking and time-reversal-preserving van Hove singularities may be exploited to achieve unique functions in the design of electronic devices. These opportunities for achieving exceptional performance may be realized through suitably tailored electron interactions within specific energy regions. These advancements provide a new path for optimizing the conductivity of pseudogapped metals, offering the potential to attain higher velocities of electrical transmission, as well as new capabilities in electronic device design. These breakthroughs in our understanding of the electronic structure of metals may also give rise to novel phenomena that can be exploited in the development of future technologies. Building beneath thick layers of rock like Aberdeen's underground tunnel provides a unique environment to research subatomic particles known as spallation neutrons. Created when high-energy cosmic particles collide with rock, these neutrons have extremely short lifespans and are difficult to detect. To study this process, scientists have designed a detection system using plastic scanners surrounded by layers of absorbing material to block background radiation. By observing the brief, radioactive signals given off by the scanners when they interact with neutrons, researchers can gather valuable information about these elusive particles. Furthermore, because the Aberdeen tunnel is situated over a deep body of water, it offers a second unique opportunity to study neutrons - those created when high-energy cosmic particles collide with the Earth's atmosphere and descend to the tunnel below. Additionally, because the surrounding rock of the tunnel is composed of solid granite, it provides a third opportunity to investigate these neutrons in a different environment. In this presentation, the design and construction of this detection system will be outlined, as well as the scientific motivations behind its creation. Additionally, discussion will be had on the plan to utilize this device in the Aberdeen tunnel laboratory to gather a long-awaited understanding of spallation neutrons. Finally, the theoretical prediction for neutron flux within the tunnel will also be shared. Unfortunately, due to scheduling constraints, a live demonstration of this device will not be possible to view during this presentation. However, I would be more than happy to answer any questions you may have in person. Lastly, if you are interested in learning more about spallation neutrons or would like to become involved in this project, please do not hesitate to reach out. I look forward to speaking with you soon. The design and construction of this detection system are the result of a collaboration between the University of Aberdeen, the University of Hertfordshire, and the University of the Witwatersrand. I would like to express my gratitude to my fellow collaborators for their hard work and dedication to this project. Now, I would like to turn the floor over to my colleague, who will be presenting on the software side of this detection system. Although not directly related to the primary focus of this presentation, our joint collaboration has enabled a level of integration that deserves mention. In the event that a neutron is detected by this detection system, a subsequent beta decay of the resulting scintillation counter may occur up to 30 seconds later. As such, we have developed a method to handle the detection of these decays in real-time using a combination of a database and an event builder.

When working with robust measures of central tendency such as the median, a suitable measure of scatter or variation is the median absolute deviation (MAD). However, traditional methods for estimating the classical MAD bias not applicable, as regular maximum likelihood estimation can introduce significant bias. This study proposes two new estimation methods for the MAD, one based on a biased estimator corrected for bias and another on an unbiased estimator, both specifically tailored for cases where the sample size is small. The proposed methods are mathematically proven to minimize bias and have been simulated with positive results. The methods have been applied to real-world data sets, showing the estimated MAD can be as reliable as the estimated scale parameter under normal distribution when sample sizes are large, despite initial biases. The method has the advantage of outperforming conventional estimation when data sets contain outliers. The R program for the proposed methods is available upon request. The methods can be adapted to other distribution functions. The traditional maximum likelihood estimator has been compared to the proposed methods for the square root of the classical MAD, called the median absolute deviation in the usual sense, with the results also included. The results show that the usual MAD has a bias closer to zero than the bias of the method for the scaled MAD, with the absolute bias of the usual MAD estimator always less than the bias of the method for the scaled MAD. The proposed methods can be useful for modeling time series, with an example application to stock prices data also included. This analysis evaluates the optimal trade-off between this increased duration and the bit error rate of the system. It is demonstrated that, under certain conditions, the optimal solution results in a higher bit error rate than a system without this diffusion. Therefore, this research aims to identify more reliable conditions for implementing this technology. The research also assesses a practical implementation of this technique in an OFDM system. The results show that the increased duration can be effectively compensated by increasing the number of subcarriers, rather than applying a direct solution to the optimal trade-off equation. We divide the prediction task into two parts: forecasting the movement pattern and predicting the actual movement itself. We propose novel models for both components, leveraging a dual representation where the prediction models both the object's motion and its three-dimensional location within a virtual environment. We utilize a spatial reasoning module with a unique circular convolution operation that considers the global motion, along with convolutional recurrent models for the temporary change, resulting in highly accurate predictions, especially for large view changes. Our method surpasses current standards in various evaluation protocols, notably exceling in forecast accuracy for big view changes. We further demonstrate that our approach generalizes well across different target views and outperforms comparison methods in real-world applications, such as action recognition and surveillance tasks. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/yuki-dk/v3p. We also introduced a new large-scale multiview evaluation dataset, NovoVid-500, featuring 500 new view video predictions scenarios, with forecast accuracy exceeding our existing knowledge, thereby posing a significant challenge for model development. The dataset is accessible via https://yuki-dk.github.io/NovoVid-500. The challenge between models and the code can be found at NovoVid Prediction Challenge 2022, hosted at https://www.cis.jhu.edu/~weiss/novicepchallenge2022/index.html. Our method's simplicity and effectiveness have inspired several further advancements, such as the integration of external data, multi-person forecasts, and light-weight models for real-time applications. These innovations' source code is also available for public use at https://github.com/yuki-dk/v3p. We have theoretically analyzed our approach's performance and proven its global optimality. Additionally, we have established a connection between our model and a well-known differential equation, along with proving a related result on prediction smoothness. Furthermore, we have designed and implemented efficient model training techniques, such as novel initialization methods, like fourier initialization, and innovative data augmentation strategies, such as temporal cycle consistency, that have resulted in robust performance across different datasets. Our method has numerous real-world applications, including the creation of realistic virtual avatars, realistic weather conditions simulation, and forecasting in surveillance, with the source code available at https://github.com/yuki-dk

This note outlines the Eisenlohr-Farris approach from 2006, focusing on determining the volume of transitive polyhedra within a given sphere in three-dimensional space. These polyhedra have the property of being fully transitive, meaning their vertices can be freely rearranged without altering their basic structure. Based on this framework, the authors developed an efficient algorithm to evaluate the total volume of all possible polyhedra meeting specific criteria within a particular sphere. The proposed method showcases the diverse application of the Fourier-Minkowski transform, often used in metrology and physics to analyze non-conventional volumes. The Fourier-Minkowski transform changes the problem of calculating a real space volume into an equivalent problem in Euclidean space, facilitating the use of geometric properties to solve the original volumetric question. The Eislenlohr-Farris method leverages this transformation to analyze the polyhedra by converting their definition into a set of constraints in Euclidean space, thereby allowing for the calculation of constrained volumes in real space. The resulting algorithm allows for the derivation of geometric constraints, such as the average or minimum/maximum volume of the polyhedra, as well as their surface area or other characteristics. Additionally, our study highlights the significance of tailored security benchmarks in the development of secure, user-friendly encryption methods. These findings hold significance across domains, serving as a reminder that the characteristics of new technologies pose novel challenges for encryption strategies. As such, it is essential to approach the design of encryption methods with flexibility and an awareness of the potential limitations of future technological advancements. In the context of our study, this means considering the potential constraints and implications of future developments on the security of our encryption methods. These lessons will prove invaluable as future technologies continue to evolve and shape the world of cryptography. This process will involve a careful examination of each protocol's underlying principle, along with a thorough assessment of its computational complexity and potential for adaptation. In the context of our study, this means that both proposed encryption schemes require careful consideration of their underlying principles, computational complexity, and the potential for adaptation to account for the limitations of new technologies. These models will serve as a benchmark for future research in this domain, as they demonstrate the key aspects to consider when designing the next generation of encryption methods.

These scenarios can be applied to scenarios such as authenticating encrypted medical images or ensuring the integrity of encrypted software. We demonstrate the applicability of our approach to the AWGN channel, including its application to quantum communications. Additionally, we investigate extensions to multi-user settings and develop novel applications for our technique. We utilized the full tight-binding model and random phase approximation to
explore flat-band plasmons in hole-doped twisted bilayer molybdenum disulfide.
Our calculations showed that lattice relaxation influences plasmon behavior.
When we considered intraband transitions, low-damped, flat plasmons emerged,
while accounting for interband transitions led to plasmon dispersion following
$\sqrt q$ law. The plasmon energies in these materials can be adjusted through
tweaking the twist angles and doping levels. For samples without lattice
relaxations, coexistence of low and high-energy plasmons occurs. Higher doping
levels however eliminate the quasi-flat plasmon. These observations imply that
two conditions must be satisfied: a flat band isolated from the other bands
and adequate doping level to witness the quasi-flat plasmon. The study offers
clues for exploring superconductivity mediated by plasmons in these materials. 
The work also provides an analytical model that can be applied to other 2D
transition metal dichalcogenides. Additionally, it highlights the relevance
of interband transitions and the limitations imposed by the Moore-Read state
Hamiltonian. Furthermore, it presents a proposal for experimenting twisted
MoS2 films doped with acceptors to observe the quasi-flat plasmons. Acceptors
can be achieved through doping p-type materials like twisted graphene or
heavily-doped MoS2. The described phenomenon is also likely to occur in other
chalcogenide materials such as twisted bilayer tungsten disulfide or
sehenide-telluride materials like Ts2, where the flat plasmons may present
differing energies due to different band structures. Experimental verification
of these findings is crucial to fully comprehend the physics underlying these
materials and to apply the proposed experiments as a means of investigation. 
The described phenomenon of the quasi-flat plasmons may also offer clues for
understanding the recently observed photonic modes in twisted bilayer materials
and present new avenues for the exploration of novel phenomena in these systems. 
The described phenomenon of the quasi-flat plasmons may also present new
challenges to the development of twisted bilayer materials used in photonic
applications and necessitates a more thorough examination of these systems. 
The study of these low-doped systems may also reveal new aspects of the physics
of the Moore-Read state and the described phenomenon of the quasi-flat plasmons.

Sequential models like LSTMs are frequently applied to process language sequences, which include inflectional patterns in verb and noun forms. We examined how well an LSTM can recognize and apply the complex morphological rules of Basque, which are characterized by irregular patterns and a high degree of fusion. Our findings show that an LSTM learned to perform tasks related to verb conjugation and noun declension, but its performance suffered due to limited knowledge of case and number information. We discovered several factors that affect an LSTM's ability to grasp these rules, which include the lack of explicit representation of grammatical case and the challenging nature of Basque's agglutinative morphology. Our study suggests that using fully embedded representations of morphological features may facilitate an LSTM's understanding of these rules. We explored various feature encoding methods, which involved combining the properties of each character in the suffixes, which led to improved performance. Our study indicates that, with appropriate data preprocessing and feature encoding methods, an LSTM can develop a useful understanding of these rules. We open-source the data used in our experiments and the code for our models, which is now part of the PyTorch Transition System Framework. Furthermore, we propose the concept of a "morphological shadow," which represents the implicit knowledge of morphological case and number information that is learned by an LSTM, which we believe is relevant to other similar tasks. We introduce a method to model this shadow, which involves a transition system that is trained in an unsupervised manner and use it to enhance the performance of an LSTM. We observed significant improvements in our experiments, which demonstrate the benefits of incorporating this model. We believe that this approach can be applied to other similar tasks, which involve the analysis of sequential language structures, such as sentence structure and part-of-speech patterns, which are all crucial for natural language understanding. Additionally, we explored another method, which involved modifying an LSTM model to include a stack-based architecture, which mimicked the structure of a parse tree. We found that this model performed better than a standard LSTM model, which we attributed to its ability to capture the "concord" relationships between the base and affixes. HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a significant 1000-fold increase in the heat it receives due to its highly eccentric 111-day orbit. As the planet rapidly moves close to its star, its surface temperature jumps dramatically from 400K to over 1400K in a matter of hours during its closest approach. Observations using the James Webb Space Telescope will soon take advantage of this planet's extraordinary environment to study various aspects of its atmosphere. Accurate information about HD80606b's orbit is crucial to making the most out of these observations. Researchers conducted in-depth analyses of the planet's transits on February 7, 2020, and December 7-8, 2021, in collaboration with the TESS spacecraft and a global network of small telescopes. Additionally, they obtained new velocity measurements which were combined with the transit data, ultimately leading to a more precise estimate of the planet's orbital path. As a result, the margin of error for predicting transit and eclipse events around HD80606b has been reduced to a matter of minutes. This new level of accuracy may allow researchers to identify potential irregularities in the planet's orbit and better prepare it for future observational studies. Furthermore, this more accurate ephemeris will facilitate the optimal scheduling of JWST observations for this planet. Researchers propose that ground-based telescopes play a vital role in refining the ephemeris of non-transiting exoplanets, particularly those like HD80606b, for which precise orbital information is crucial. This is especially important given that a single day of high-cadence data is often more valuable than a week's worth of regular observations. To this end, they suggest developing strategies and protocols for coordinating ground-based and space-based observations of exoplanets in order to make the most out of these valuable resources. As a testament to the effectiveness of these approaches, the most recent analysis of the HD80606b data has been selected as the "Alert System Success Story" in the recently published "Scientific Opportunities with the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite" book. This measurement is typically done using the neutron detection method, where a measurement of the total cross-section of neutrons and plastic scintillator is a crucial step. This study presents a novel 3D-projection method for identifying and analyzing events, leading to an enhanced measurement of the total cross-section with reduced systematic errors. Compared to conventional methods, this approach exhibits improved performance in event selection, background rejection, and stability correction, allowing for a more precise measurement. As a result, the measured total cross-section of neutrons and plastic scintillator at 88% confidence level is 0.323±0.028 barn, indicating that this method is highly effective for the neutron detection method. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the capability of the 3D-projection method to measure the neutron lifetime, resulting in a value of 0.657±0.051 microseconds, which is compatible with the established value but with greater precision. This study also investigates the 3D distribution of events and reveals that the currently adopted one-dimensional model is conservative, resulting in a relatively large systematic error. Therefore, it is recommended that the development of sophisticated models, such as the proposed three-dimensional model, be considered for the measurement of the neutron decay rate in plastic scintillator. Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush behavior have provided valuable insights into the spatial arrangement of attached polymers and the impact of their size and distribution on surface and interfacial properties. However, the paradigm of these theories, which often assumes a perfectly uniform and spacious brush base, does not account for areas around the edges where polymers cannot extend due to steric constraints. We have mathematically modeled the excluded space around the edges of strongly stretched brushes with arbitrary shapes and investigated its implications on chain statistics and brush properties. We demonstrate that considering this excluded space can significantly alter chain conformation and lead to increased free energy compared to models ignoring it's impact. Furthermore, we identify the conditions under which the excluded volume effect becomes negligible, and show that it potentially plays a crucial role in the phase behavior of colloid-polymer mixtures at interfaces. This work sets the stage for further exploration of how the excluded space affects other complex systems. We also propose the term "end exclusion area" to describe these constrained spaces in molecular dynamics. Additionally, we have numerically validated our analytical models using simulations based on open system and closure approaches, and have made our simulation code publicly available for others to use. We expect this work to contribute meaningfully to the better understanding of brush chain behavior and to facilitate further research into other complex systems. Nonetheless, we acknowledge a limitation of our research, where the broad applicability of our findings is assumed solely within the scope of strong-stretched brush chains. Therefore, we encourage others to build upon and extend this research. Finally, we have formally analyzed but numerically cannot fully resolve the issue of how excluded space impacts the phase diagrams of colloid-polymer mixtures, and thus consider this aspect of this research as ongoing. The Southern Atlantic rift basin formed as a divergent margin during the Jurassic and Cretaceous periods as two supercontinents, Gondwana and Laurasia, moved apart.  Despite extensive mapping, modeling, and analysis of magnetic anomalies, the early history of the rift basin remains somewhat unclear due to the limited resolution of seismic data and the complexity of geological time scales.  Recent improvements in seismic reflection data, combined with updated time scales, allow for a reevaluation of the rift basin's early development.  This reevaluation identifies three distinct phases in the basin's formation.  Initially, rifting occurred at ~185 million years ago during the early Toarcian as a narrow, E-W oriented trough.  However, this initial phase was followed by significant changes; the rifting pattern broadened and the basin shifted towards a NE-SW orientation with numerous faults.  Furthermore, sedimentary deposits that dated back to ~183 million years ago during the Pliensbachian had been uplifted and eroded, indicating that rifting had occurred over a substantial period of at least 2 million years.  During this time, extensional crustal thinning led to low-angle normal faulting and the formation of a domal structure.  This domal structure eventually gave way to continental break-up that occurred around ~125 million years ago during the Aptian as Albian sea-spread towards Brazil and ~125.5 million years ago towards South Africa.  This break-up marked the beginning of two separate passive margins with distinct magmatic and metamorphic provinces on either side.  These margins then experienced thermal subsidence and epeirogenic uplift that shaped the sedimentary deposits, ultimately resulting in the present-day morphology of the Southern Atlantic rift basin.  This review of the rift basin's history also highlights the significant differences between the South American and African margins, providing valuable insights for future modeling and analysis of this significant geological feature. A proven strategy in image processing is information maximization, particularly in segments like image segmentation, where making the most of available information is crucial. This approach typically involves creating dummy tasks to challenge the model, thus making the most of the data it has been trained on. A primary challenge with this method is often the significant difference between the difficulty level of the dummy tasks and the actual task at hand. If the model performs well on the dummy tasks but struggles with the real task, it may indicate that it has learned how to take advantage of the given data, but still, there is a significant amount of valuable information that the model is not utilizing. To address this shortcoming, we propose a new framework that combines two techniques: first, we add noise to the dummy tasks to prevent the model from overfitting on easy tasks and, second, we incorporate boundary-sensitive cross-entropy loss into the optimization objective to encourage the model to pay attention to data boundaries. The model's performance is evaluated on three public datasets, and the results show that our proposed method outperforms the baseline models. Additionally, our method's ability to produce models that generalize well is demonstrated through pilot clinical validation studies. The code for our framework is available online. We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines automated Dungeon Master roles with a learning framework based on Providence Network modules, which are trained using player interactions and goal-oriented conversations. We leverage this approach to demonstrate the potential for a Dungeon Master to teach Theory-of-Mind concepts through repeated gaming sessions, with results showing that players learn essential aspects of these complex mental processes. Moreover, we explore various aspects of the G4C setting, including the effects of different identity expressions and the importance of a consistent Dungeon Master tone. Overall, our research highlights the efficacy of Dungeons and Dragons as a platform for assessing and refining human learning through natural language interactions. Finally, we introduce the open-source D4C framework, which enables researchers to design and execute their own gaming sessions, as well as integrate existing Providence Network applications with the underlying Dungeon Master codebase. With this framework, we aim to contribute to the development of more advanced role-playing games that can monitor and direct natural language interactions in line with predefined goals and objectives. Furthermore, we invite other researchers to collaborate with us on the G4C challenge. Additionally, we have incorporated a new element, known as the D4C Subworld, which represents a miniature, issue-based environment within the larger Dungeons and Dragons setting. This Subworld can serve as either a challenging problem for the player character to resolve or a character trait that influences their behavior. We have also introduced several new elements to the D4C dataset, consisting of over 2,500 new multi-turn dialog conversations derived from actual Dungeons and Dragons campaigns, as well as accompanying goal descriptions and associated Theory-of-Mind graphs capturing the underlying intentions and mental states behind the players' actions. Complex lexical semantic relationships among words are the foundation for numerous NLP tasks, which typically rely on pre-built knowledge bases and typically assume a binary, two-way semantic connection between words. In contrast, our proposed variation discovery model allows for the inference of multi-way semantic relationships among words. By leveraging and extending the syntactic and lexical patterns present in WordNet, we develop a graphical representation of lexical semantics based on hypergraphs. This model serves as a starting point for our word pair similarity learner, which utilizes a binary decision tree to distinguish between related and unrelated word pairs while ignoring any additional information. To investigate the capacity of our model to capture complex semantic relationships, we conduct a series of experiments using data sourced from online forums and Wikipedia articles. Our results demonstrate that our model is capable of identifying both fundamental and intricate semantic relationships among words. Furthermore, we showcase the applicability of our model by utilizing the learned representations to perform three diverse NLP tasks: text classification, semantic analogy tasks, and machine translation. Our approach proves particularly effective when compared to other state-of-the-art methods, and our code is now publicly available for public use. Our model's versatility, where the decision tree's structure represents the underlying lexical semantic relationships among words, enables a range of applications while also providing a useful representation for words that can be employed in a variety of NLP tasks. Additionally, we introduce the WordNetGraph dataset, a set of hypergraph representations of lexical semantics based on WordNet, which can be utilized for further research in this domain. This dataset comprises 883 unique concepts, which are organized through 114 distinct parent concepts, and features 31 concepts that serve as universal "roots," thereby providing a foundation for the development of future models. We propose introducing a new class of distribution functions tied to $k_\perp$ that differ from the standard Bose-Einstein distribution. These functions are connected to the behavior of quasiparticles in the medium and are dependent on the direction of motion relative to the medium's flow direction. Unlike the Bose-Einstein distribution, they do not follow the principle of detailed balance, which results in the appearance of dispersion relations that deviate from the standard form, $\omega = k$. Additionally, we show that one of the proposed distribution functions leads to a $1 + \ln(1 + \frac{\omega}{T})$ dispersion and that it causes the dispersion relation to shift from $\omega = k$, while another proposed distribution function results in a $\sqrt{\omega^2 - k^2}$ dispersion. These dependent distribution functions are applicable in thermodynamic equilibrium or non-equilibrium situations and are relevant for describing the properties of Bose and Fermi systems within a medium. They provide a means for incorporating quasiparticle dispersion relations that are consistent with the Jost flat cut in the complex frequency plane in scenarios where the quasiparticle's rest frame is not aligned with the medium's flow frame. Additionally, we offer a new approach for summing over these dependent distribution functions within the thermodynamic potential $\Omega$, which yields unique quasiparticle densities that account for the distortion caused by the motion through the medium. This leads to revised expressions for the energy density, pressure, and speed of sound within a Bose or Fermi system, resulting in values that differ from their equilibrium-form counterparts. We also provide a new definition for the effective mass of a quasiparticle and show that it varies depending on the angle between the quasiparticle's direction of motion and the flow direction of the medium. This new mass definition is relevant for describing the behavior of particles moving through a medium, especially in high-energy particle physics experiments where the energy and angle of the scattered particles are critical in determining the appropriate mass of the particle of interest. We anticipate these dependent distribution functions to be instrumental in furthering our understanding of hadron physics within a quark-gluon plasma and expect them to contribute to the development of new approaches for describing the properties of quasiparticles in quantum statistics. To resolve the $H_0$ discrepancy, early dark energy (EDE) has been proposed with various models suggesting similar implications for the Hubble constant. Despite hissing criticisms about the ad hoc nature of such models, researchers investigated how well EDE models align with $H_0$ values derived from Planck and Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey data, utilizing a statistical method called the profile likelihood. By employing this method, researchers discovered a more stringent constraint on EDE than previously reported, with a starting density parameter $\log_{10}(f-1)=-2.68\pm0.36$ at the photon decoupling epoch, resulting in a 95% confidence interval for the present-day density parameter $\Omega_{\rm EDE}(0.5H_0^{-1})=0.015\pm0.021$, and implying little impact on $\Omega_{\rm total}(z=0.5)$. Furthermore, researchers found that within this range, the primary indication of EDE is consistent with observed features in the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest and cosmic microwave background anisotropies. Additionally, a simple cross-check using a different statistical method yielded similar outcomes, providing $f-1\sim\exp(-2.75\pm0.37)$. Notably, both approaches indicate that if EDE is present, it must begin very early in the universe's evolution, with its density parameter at the photon decoupling epoch already quite substantial, thus implying significant implications for the universe's early history and potential connections to fundamental theories. Moreover, researchers discovered that such a dense, early energy component with these characteristics may raise issues with the universe's stability during the photon decoupling epoch and in its late stages, with a potential impact on neutrino fluctuations and large-scale structure formation. Nonetheless, further investigation is needed to fully determine the universe's early energy composition and its lasting effects on the universe's evolution. Additionally, researchers propose future observations, such as the Planck legacy mission, the Dark Energy Survey, BOSS, X-CDM, and the Atacama Large Millimeter-wave Array, among others, will provide more precise constraints on EDE models. Nonetheless, researchers warn that regardless of the outcome, it is essential to address the inherent methodological limitations and statistical pitfalls inherent in such analyses. Finally, future studies should explore comprehensive model-independent analyses and cross-checks using multiple observations and methodologies to accurately determine how well EDE models fit the data. To address this limitation, we develop a technique to distill the phrasal hypotheses generated by these models, aiming to produce more coherent and informative responses. Through extensive evaluations, our approach demonstrates substantial enhancements over baseline models and eliminates the disparity in performance between self-evaluation and human assessment. Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise for advancing semiconductor technology through strain engineering and novel material synthesis. Despite challenges, recent studies have made notable breakthroughs, primarily involving the growth of binary semiconductors, but there is a lack of systematic analysis on the epitaxial relationships in Heusler compounds, which possess unique electronic properties and are used in spintronics and thermoelectric applications. In this study, a comprehensive examination is conducted on the epitaxial relationships of La-Fe-Si Heusler films grown on graphene/sapphire substrates, involving a comprehensive analysis of their structural, magnetic, and electrical characteristics. The results show that La-Fe-Si Heusler films can be synthesized through remote epitaxy with a (111) orientation, but only when a thin ferrimagnetic layer forms on the substrate, which serves as a nucleation layer for strain relief. Changing the substrate to graphene/BaAlO$_3$ leads to a (110) oriented Heusler film with improved magnetic properties and conductivity, but results in a mixed epitaxial structure comprising both pinhole and van der Waals growth regions. Notably, the van der Waals growth is characterized by a ferrimagnetic layer with negative magnetoresistance, which is normally absent in bulk Heusler compounds. The unique properties of these films make them suitable for thermoelectric applications and the unique epitaxial structure offers a potential solution to the challenge of achieving remote epitaxy. Additionally, this study demonstrates the effectiveness of La-Fe-Si Heusler films grown on graphene/sapphire substrates as biosensors. The results indicate that these films exhibit high sensitivity to molecular substances like tryptophan and lysozyme, but only when they are grown through a van der Waals process. Furthermore, La-Fe-Si Heusler films grown on graphene/BaAlO$_3$ substrates are found to be highly resistant to degradation when used as biosensors and offer a relatively high figure of merit, but only when they are operated at low temperatures. The findings of this study provide a comprehensive understanding of the epitaxial relationships in Heusler compounds and the characteristics of their electronic and magnetic properties, which can be modified through strain engineering. The results also indicate that La-Fe-Si Heusler films grown on graphene/sapphire and graphene/BaAlO$_3$ substrates have great potential for a variety of applications, including spintronics, thermoelectric applications, and bios

We specifically examine the dimension of the kernel in the case where $p=2$. Additionally, we propose two decoding algorithms, both applicable to codes over the binary field. One of these algorithms, suitable for $\mathbb{Z}_2\mathbb{Z}_4$-linear codes with a specific type of automorphism, can be viewed as a semilinear decoding algorithm. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our decoding algorithms through an explicit example. Furthermore, we investigate the relationship between $\mathbb{Z}_2\mathbb{Z}_4$-linear codes and their corresponding quadratic codes. We propose two potential constructions for binary codes associated with a message, and we examine the parity-check matrices of the resulting codes. We also examine the dimension of the kernel of these codes and provide a description of the kernel in a specific case. Lastly, we explore potential future research directions in the field of $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes. We comment on the suitability of these codes for practice and suggest several open problems await solution. Furthermore, we propose two general decoding strategies for $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes and outline two possible approaches to implementing these strategies. We also examine the applicability of these strategies to various types of codes, such as self-dual codes and Hamming codes. We discuss the implications of these decoding strategies for code design and propose several open problems related to the field of $\mathbb{Z}_p\mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$-linear codes. The success of supervised learning models heavily relies on high-quality labeled data, which are expensive and time-consuming to create. One costly step in this process is data annotation, where each sample is assigned a single label despite often being relevant to multiple categories. This paper proposes a method to automatically generate relevant multi-label samples based on a single annotation, reducing annotation costs and potentially utilizing existing single-annotated data sets more effectively. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through an annotation-assisted learning framework, which incorporates previously annotated data and uses the proposed method to train models on previously unannotated samples. The results show that even with limited annotated data, the proposed method outperforms traditional annotation methods and improves model performance on relevant multi-label tasks. The advantages of this approach are illustrated using natural language processing and computer vision data sets.
