The connection between low-energy radio and high-energy gamma-ray emissions in nearby galaxies has long been a mystery.  Recent studies suggest that gamma-ray emission is associated with relativistic jets in these galaxies; however, it is unclear why some jets exhibit gamma-ray radiation while others do not.  Analyzing a comprehensive sample of 59 nearby radio galaxies, we discovered that gamma-ray detection is correlated with jets that have narrow bends, as evidenced by magnetic field observations.  In contrast, wide bends in these jets are not linked to gamma-ray detection.  This phenomenon may arise because narrow bends cause particles to accelerate more quickly in accretion disks, resulting in the production of gamma-rays.  Our research implies that gamma-rays in these jets can be understood through a multi-messy framework, where magnetic restrictions play a crucial role in particle acceleration and the production of high-energy gamma-rays.  Furthermore, our study reveals that hadronic energy production in these jets exceeds that of relativistic electrons, thus providing valuable insights into the composition and absorption processes in these galaxies.  Lastly, since hadronic processes can generate gamma-rays, the non-detection of gamma-rays in certain jets may be an indication of the presence of a blocking object, such as a foreground galaxy, rather than the absence of a jet.  Consequently, accounting for hadronic processes and magnetic restrictions in these jets is essential for a complete understanding of these systems.  Additionally, our research opens up intriguing possibilities for the study of particle acceleration, gamma-ray production, and hidden blocking objects in these powerful astrophysical jets.  Furthermore, considering the constraints imposed by hadronic processes and gamma-ray production, a re-examination of existing and future high-energy studies is also recommended.  In effect, our study provides a groundbreaking foundation for a novel theoretical framework that can be applied not only to the analysis of radio galaxies but also to other multi-messy phenomena in the universe.  Consequently, we propose a new model dubbed "Restricted Disk Model" that can be applied to a wide range of situations and we anticipate that our study and its results will spark innovative ideas and a fresh perspective on these complex phenomena in the universe.  Lastly, as our research theory suggests the presence of blocking objects such as foreground galaxies, it is our belief that this study will serve as a catalyst for a wave of blockage-related studies in the field of astrophysics.  Therefore, we are confident that our study and its findings will have a lasting impact and provide a groundbreaking foundation on which future research can be built.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate diagnosis via auscultation is impaired by poor sound quality resulting from noise and the distortion of cardiac sounds. To address this challenge, this study develops a robust method for categorizing cardiac sounds into normal and abnormal sounds, even in the presence of noise and distortion.  Initially, cardiac sounds are recorded from multiple sources, including patients with valve problems and healthy individuals, totalling 1500 sounds of 10 seconds duration.  Twenty experts classify these sounds into normal or abnormal sounds.  To train the classifier, cardiac sounds are corrupted with different types of noise and passed through a virtual stethoscope, mimicking the distortion caused by it being heard through a medical device.  A convolutional neural network, trained with cardiac sounds classified by experts, delivers a high classification accuracy even in the presence of noise and distortion.  When tested with undistorted cardiac sounds, the network achieves an impressive 95% accuracy, surpassing human experts.  When tested with cardiac sounds resembling those heard through a stethoscope, it achieves a 90% accuracy, a significant improvement over previous methods.  Furthermore, this method facilitates real-time classification.  To validate the method, recordings taken with the developed system are compared with those obtained with an high-end electronic stethoscope, revealing no difference in sound quality.  Finally, the system is utilised to detect mitral valve problems, achieving an accuracy of 80% compared to clinical diagnoses, providing a viable non-invasive alternative for diagnosing heart conditions. Additionally, this method may be adapted for interpreting sounds from other bodily organs.  Furthermore, cardiac sound data generated in this study is also made available for the broader research community.  Ultimately, this study offers a groundbreaking solution for accurately diagnosing heart conditions via auscultation, even in poor sound quality conditions.  To further improve the method, consideration should be given to incorporating expert classifications based on condition type or recording location.  Additionally, future systems incorporating both visual and auditory feedback may enhance diagnostic accuracy even more. Ultimately, we believe that MadDog represents a significant step forward in the development of an acronym Disambiguation system, capable of efficiently handling a vast acronym database across several language varieties and contexts. To tackle this challenge, our proposed MAG-Net integrates two unique systems. The image-processing component is a multi-task directed network that uses attention mechanisms to focus on critical areas within the MRI scan, while the report-processing module is a recursive neural network that models the radial relationships within the text. The two integrated systems allow for the combination of visual and textual information, with the result that MAG-Net outperforms the competition. Experimental results show that our proposed model achieves impressive accuracy in classifying brain tumors on the BRATS2013 dataset. Furthermore, by integrating the model with an MRI scan and radiologists' report, a 97% accuracy rate is achieved in classifying a specific brain tumor test case. By automatically generating point clouds from 2D maps, we can increase the size and diversity of available data without the need for expensive and time-consuming real-world scans. Despite the appeal of this approach, currently available methods for converting map representations into point clouds are complex and cannot be efficiently optimized using standard differentiable optimization techniques. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel shadow-based algorithm for accurately modeling scene geometry and precisely calculating point clouds from map representations. This shadow-based algorithm leverages techniques from semi-analytical integration and rejection sampling to efficiently convert 2D maps into accurate 3D point clouds. By utilizing this model in an optimization framework, we can train and refine the algorithm using gradient-based updates, even in the presence of noisy and misaligned map data. By applying this technique to a real-world dataset, we demonstrate significant improvements in the accuracy of our 3D predictions and show that the algorithm can successfully predict point clouds on unseen scenes. Furthermore, we find that the algorithm exhibits robust performance in the face of varying map resolutions and noise levels. The developed algorithm serves as a versatile tool for converting 2D maps into 3D point clouds and can be incorporated into end-to-end training pipelines for navigation systems. In the study of population dynamics, identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and eventual collapse is a complex challenge. This study tackles this issue by examining the long-term behavior of a two-timescale ecosystem model featuring a predator that switches between two prey species. The model's unique characteristics include the possibility of predator coexistence with both prey species, as well as the exclusion of one prey species by the other. A method was developed to analyze the model's stability near a stable, oscillatory equilibrium and the resulting boundary was found. The location of this boundary was found to indicate the onset of rapid, irreversible population changes in the predator. Conditions for the model's internal persistence equilibrium to be locally asymptotically stable were also established, and an analysis of a related model without switching was conducted to gain insights into the persistence equilibrium's location and the model's internal stability. The results provide a framework for addressing the challenge of identifying early warning indicators for sudden population changes and eventual collapse. The study is a theoretical examination of a specific predator-prey model, but the methods developed could be applied to other two-timescale models featuring switching dynamics. This paper delves into the relationship detection task, identifying a significant issue that most current top-performing models encounter: they incorrectly associate certain entities. Our analysis indicates that the conventional evaluation metrics, AUC and AR, are insufficiently rigorous, as they do not account for incorrect associations. To address this shortcoming, we propose novel evaluation metrics, including the use of precision and F1 score for evaluation, which reflect real-world applications more accurately. Furthermore, we introduce a method to segment relationships within a single image, demonstrating lower precision and higher false positive rates compared to existing benchmarks. To mitigate the prevalence of incorrect associations, we explore various data augmentation techniques and establish a new baseline models before presenting two primary strategies to reduce incorrect associations: (1) employing contrastive learning to differentiate between similar and distinct entities and (2) incorporating entity manipulation techniques in photorealistic scenarios. Our research demonstrates the complexity of the relationship detection task and highlights the importance of stringent evaluation protocols and sophisticated models in accurately identifying visual relationships. Our code and data have been made publicly available at https://github.com/zwang84/Visual-Relationship-Detection-Challenges. Our findings also suggest potential applications beyond detection, such as improving entity localization through the reduction of false positives and the enhancement of model interpretability by reducing model size through the removal of false positive relationships. Our analysis has been further summarized into an infographic available at https://www.google.com/search?q=visual+relationship+detection&spell=1&sa=X&ved=0ahUKEwjZ5O3Z5O7uAhXO6H0KHQvAD3AQ8iCQ. Moreover, our research has been presented in a video available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=6Q5C0q4D2QY. Overall, this paper emphasizes the necessity to address the issue of incorrect associations in visual relationship detection and proposes several techniques and data augmentation methods capable of mitigating this problem. Our research demonstrates the value of sophisticated evaluation metrics, along with the potential applications of false positive reduction in entity manipulation, contrastive learning, and model interpretability. Our findings have been verified through extensive experiments and we believe that our work will contribute meaningfully to the advancement of relationship detection models. Our research has been further validated through a survey conducted among renowned relationship detection researchers, whose insights have been outlined in the appendix of this paper. Our analysis has been graphically represented in various visualization tools, including tables, figures, and infographics, which have been embedded within the text

Current neural code editors can accurately make small changes to existing code but often struggle with more significant transformations, such as expanding code loops and functions. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new approach that leverages static code analysis to help the model better understand code structure and generate more complex extensions. Using a code analysis tool called ABCD, we develop a system that provides neural code editors with three valuable tools: verified program checks, suggested modifications, and underlying program abstractions. By building upon the foundation of the ABCD tool suite, we create a set of program transformations that can be used as preconditions for the neural code editor, ensuring that the generated code is valid and consistent with the original code, as well as facilitating easier code analysis and understanding. With this approach, we demonstrate improved code generation capabilities and a significant boost in code validity, when compared to a baseline neural code editor model that relies solely on natural language instructions for guidance. We also explore the potential of dynamic code abstractions to provide additional context to the model, enabling it to generate more accurate and reliable code transformations. By integrating our system with the NeRF code editor model, we observe a notable increase in code validity and a more manageable error rate, when the model is tasked with creating complex code from natural language descriptions. We make the source code for our static analysis-based code editor available online. With this approach, we anticipate significant performance gains for large-scale code generation tasks, particularly in domains with limited amounts of training data, due to the ability to efficiently utilize existing static code analyses with neural code editors. In particular, our results indicate a 12% points boost in code validity for the Python language, a 16% points boost in MATLAB, and a 10% points boost in PHP, when compared to baseline models. Additionally, we explore the interplay between program structure and natural language, by conducting a qualitative analysis of multiple case studies, when neural code editors struggle to accurately generate code from natural language descriptions. We use these insights to inform our design of a more effective neural code editor model, that is better able to generate accurate code from natural language descriptions, particularly in complex scenarios, and facilitate the integration of static code analyses with such models, leading to significant improvements in code validity, when compared to state-of-the-art baseline models. Our team utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for integral field unit (IFU) observations of 9 ultra/luminous infrared galaxies located close to our own (z < 0.04) and participating in the GOALS survey. These targets span a broad spectrum of merger phases, from early stages to advanced. With the IFU data we collected, we successfully isolated several distinct emission lines including hydrogen beta, oxygen III at wavelength 5007, hydrogen alpha, double-ionized nitrogen at wavelengths 6549, 6583, and sulfur II at wavelengths 6717, 6731. Our analysis with spectral resolutions ranging between 1500 to 2000 allowed us to derive spatially resolved ionized gas maps as small as 200-700 parsecs, as well as active galactic nucleus (AGN) diagnostics within 3-11 kiloparsecs of our targets. Our data show a correlation between active galactic nuclei and the outflow of gas as oxygen III, a trend that is (1) most prevalent in the centers of galaxies and (2) stronger at later stages of merger. For example, during late stages of merger we measured an outflow 1.5 times as powerful as during early stages of merger. These observations imply a relationship between the interaction of galaxy mergers and the outflow of gas that is likely induced by active supermassive black holes. Optimistically, our findings could serve as a marker to identify distant active supermassive black holes that may be causing gas to flow out of galaxies across the universe. Due to the relatively low spatial resolution of Seimei Telescope's KOOLS-IFU, our detection rate of gas flow was lower than expected, leading us to hypothesize that with more sensitive and highly advanced optical IFU on ground-based telescopes such as the LTAO/MAIO on Subaru Telescope, we could successfully detect a far more substantial number of active supermassive black holes in our own galaxy and elsewhere. As a result, we propose a theoretical relationship between the mass of a supermassive black hole and the power of a gas flow-induced optical line, which we aim to validate with upcoming observations from far more sensitive and cutting-edge instruments. Until then, we will rely on theoretical models such as the use of radiative transfer simulations to interpret our current data and demonstrate the widely accepted theory that a supermassive black hole plays a crucial role in causing the flow of gas as observed in the optical spectrum of galaxies. Notably, models performing exceptionally well on the dataset may lack effectiveness in real-world scenarios due to the ease with which they overfit the data. Consequently, our study emphasizes the significance of retaining a balanced approach, incorporating both sophisticated architectures and straightforward models, to gain a comprehensive understanding of this challenging computer vision domain. In conclusion, this study provides a lasting impact on the development of computer vision models tailored to real-world applications through its emphasis on practical, balanced evaluations. Additionally, our findings are applicable across a broad spectrum of image classification contexts. Nonetheless, further research is needed to fully grasp the intricate dynamics of this vision domain due to the consistently observed drop in accurate classifications as model complexity increases. Nonetheless, our study paves the way for subsequent investigations into more intricate weather conditions, such as cloudy days with light precipitation, as well as the development of models centered on context-driven approaches, leveraging information pertaining to the time of day, location, and image contents. Lastly, our study raises the crucial question of incorporating external knowledge into model training, along with potential solutions to the significant challenge of annotating datasets on a larger scale. The study utilizes a reduced number of fluid simulations to mimic the behavior of multiple layers. The study also indicates that the choice of control variables significantly impacts the results, leading to various scenarios in which either the traditional approach or the multi-fluid model yields more accurate results. Ultimately, the research suggests that the multi-fluid model is the more reliable of the two options. Reinforcement learning agents can achieve optimal performance in complex tasks by imitating expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations becomes impractical due to the extensive labeling required. This paper introduces a new training method called Co-Imitation, where agents learn from each other's experiences without the need for expert demonstrations. Co-Imitation learning involves two distinct components: agent pairing and update rules. When two agents with similar skills are paired together, they receive the same reward signals and independently adapt their policies to maximize expected returns. As they interact with each other, their behavior converges to a state of mutual imitation. We demonstrate that not only does co-imitation learning succeed in mimicking the strongest agent but also that it outperforms single-agent training in several benchmark tasks by achieving better performance and stability. The code for these experiments is publicly available on GitHub. Despite its efficient use of labeling, co-imitation learning remains effective even when the agent pair is not optimally aligned, making it a promising learning framework. Its potential advantages over existing methods that rely on expert demonstrations or diverse data sets need further exploration.

MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented, distributed NoSQL database that allows for three different isolation levels in its client interactions: snapshot, snapshot with conflict resolution, and snapshot with conflict resolution and rollback. To facilitate formal verification, we have developed a formal model representing MongoDB's transactional coherence, specifically for version-based isolation. This model is part of a larger proof consisting of three lemmas that demonstrate the consistency of MongoDB's transactional coherence with respect to its specification of transactional behavior, as well as a demonstration of how this model can be verified using the Coq proof assistant. This work contributes a key finding to the field of database verification: specifically, we have shown that MongoDB's transactional coherence can be verified to be consistent with respect to its specified transactional behavior. This achievement demonstrates the effectiveness of using formal verification to prove the correctness of a database's concurrency control system. Additionally, we have incorporated an interactive tutorial into this proof, which provides a step-by-step guide on how to verify MongoDB's transactional coherence using the Coq proof assistant. This tutorial can serve as a valuable resource for teaching students about the process of verifying database correctness. Furthermore, we have also explored the application of this verification approach to other databases, successfully verifying the transactional coherence of Redis's Redis-Transactions. Thanks to advancements in computer networks and artificial intelligence, emotionally rich interactions with virtual assistants have become more engaging and effective. Successful emotional connections with these systems rely heavily on their ability to accurately detect the user's emotions. Although deep learning-based emotion recognition systems perform well on standardized evaluation datasets, they struggle with adaptability when applied to real-world data. In this research, we explore adapting deep reinforcement learning for data preprocessing to enhance the performance of speech emotion recognition systems. Initial results demonstrate that this approach yields superior performance when adapting to new data and a more stable baseline when adapting to new domains. Our method, which we call Reinforcement Learning-based Preprocessing (RlPP), incorporates a pre-trained classifier and a reinforcement learning agent within a preprocessing loop. RlPP uses a transition system to select preprocessing parameters and a learning agent to prioritize transformations that improve classification accuracy. In our experiments, we evaluate RlPP's performance across multiple datasets and find that it achieves state-of-the-art classification accuracy in speech emotion recognition. Furthermore, we apply RlPP to a real-world virtual assistant dataset and discover that it surpasses industry-standard baseline performance. Second, we plan to integrate RlPP with popular deep learning-based speech analysis models like Convolutional Neural Networks and Residual Neural Networks. Lastly, we are interested in applying RlPP to other audio-related tasks like source separation and synthesis. We present an investigation of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ (BFTO), a four-layer Aurivillius compound, under the influence of high hydrostatic pressure.  Our findings indicate that BFTO initially exhibits antiferromagnetic behavior under pressure but transitions to a ferromagnetic state above 8 GPa.  This behavior is further supported by nuclear forward scattering and magnetic characterization using a vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM).  Notably, the switch from antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic ordering results in a notable increase in magnetic moment as evidenced by the pressure dependence of the normalized counts in our nuclear forward scattering spectra.  To further understand this transition, we performed first-principle calculations which predict a significant shortening of the Fe-O bond length under pressure, potentially inducing local spin fluctuations that could drive this magnetic transition.  Nonetheless, the exact mechanism behind this transition remains subject to ongoing investigation and future study.  We propose that Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ could serve as a suitable model system for exploring the physics underlying magnetic transitions induced by applied pressure.  Finally, we recommend investigating other members of the Aurivillius compound series using both experimental and theoretical approaches to gain a deeper understanding of the unique properties exhibited by these materials.  Additionally, we suggest considering the effects of pressure on the structural parameters of these materials and propose that the application of electrical pressure could provide valuable insights, potentially paving the way for future studies incorporating both electrical and mechanical pressure in materials research.  As such, we hope to contribute to the advancement of theoretical models describing the physics underlying pressure-induced magnetic transitions in complex materials.  Furthermore, we hope to stimulate further investigation into the properties of Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ and related compounds through the continued application of nuclear forward scattering in combination with magnetic characterization and first-principle calculations.  As such, we look forward to contributing to the progress of materials research and the development of new theoretical models in this field. Multiple studies have analyzed the performance of randomly assembled low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes under various error-prone environments, including binary erasure channels and noise, as well as scenarios with mixed types of errors. Nonetheless, researchers have given limited attention to the effects of degree-degree correlations within these LDPC codes. In contrast, we investigate how degree-degree correlations influence the overall performance of LDPC codes when transmitted over a binary deletion channel. Furthermore, we discuss the methods for constructing ensembles of LDPC codes that incorporate degree-degree correlations and exhibit optimized error-correction capabilities. Numerical simulations demonstrate the significant improvements achieved with degree-degree correlated LDPC code ensembles over their standard, independently assembled counterparts, with some code ensembles exhibiting a 10 dB improvement in signal-to-no-error rate. Moreover, we explore the implications of these findings for the design of degree-degree correlated LDPC codes. In particular, we observe that in scenarios where the rate of deletions significantly differs from the maximum tolerance of these codes, the best strategy is to assemble LDPC codes using commonly employed anti-aliasing techniques available in digital signal processing, thereby regaining much of the gained performance. In contrast, we find that in scenarios where the rate of deletions approaches the code's maximum tolerance, the most advantageous degree-degree correlated codes are those with a positive correlation between low-degree nodes and high-degree nodes. In future research, we plan to examine in greater depth various other forms of node correlations. In addition, we aim to investigate more complex structural characteristics of LDPC codes, as well as their performance under other types of error-prone environments. In such settings, the binary deletion channel approximates these environments with fewer errors, making it an essential intermediate step in the development of more complex communication protocols. Lastly, we anticipate that the techniques and methodologies for assembling degree-degree correlated LDPC code ensembles will also prove useful in furthering our understanding of other decoding algorithms that rely on iterative node-to-node message passing, such as those employed in decoding quantum LDPC codes and in inference tasks within graphical models. In these contexts, the introduction of node correlations may bypass the limitations imposed by the random ensemble assembly methodology, thereby enabling a more in-depth examination of the fundamental boundaries of these codes' error-correcting capabilities. In doing so, we may uncover novel strategies for optimizing the performance of these communication protocols. In such cases, the four-dimensional performance landscape, defined by three dimensions of node degrees and a density dimension, may serve as a critical platform for the development of cutting-edge communication technologies

A critical flaw exists in the decoy-state method, commonly employed for quantum key distribution (QKD), which involves attacking the system with a technique called hacking. Although various improvements have been proposed to enhance the security of QKD, none have addressed the fundamental limitation imposed by the phase randomization process. In this research, we identify the critical component that facilitates hacking, which is shown to be thwarted by incorporating a randomly changed phase in each system and source laser, thereby necessitating the development of a new attack strategy. Subsequently, we demonstrate and analyze the efficacy of this attack in various scenarios. Notably, our findings reveal that even with the incorporation of randomly changed phases, hacking can yield an average of 10^12 bits, which far exceeds the optimal performance of the conventional phase-encoding strategy. Moreover, we investigate the stress placed on quantum channels by various system configurations and demonstrate that the optimal performance is achieved with low-intensity laser, whereas the highest hacking efficiency is obtained with highly intense laser. Lastly, we observe that the optimal performance and highest hacking efficiency can be achieved with very low and extremely high number of system participants respectively. In essence, our findings imply that the optimal performance and highest hacking efficiency can be realized without the knowledge of quantum channel conditions. In conclusion, our research provides invaluable insights into the workings of hacking in QKD systems and highlights the significance of understanding the impact of phase randomization. Finally, we conclude by emphasizing the necessity for the development of novel, decoy-state-free methods that can safeguard QKD systems from hacking. Recent observations suggest that in some T Tauri star systems, magnetic fields are weakly anchored to their surrounding disks. Additionally, advanced numerical models have revealed that dying stars can generate massive shocks within these disks, leading to the production of magnetic field-aligned jets. However, these models fail to account for the long-term behavior of these shocks and the production of jets. This paper presents a revised model, demonstrating that self-sustaining vortex rings can form within these disks due to a combination of their fast rotation, narrow width, and the pressure they exert on the surrounding disk material. As a result, a significant amount of the star's angular momentum becomes trapped within these rings, creating channels for further material accumulation. This process sets the stage for the formation of multiple protoplanets within a planetary system. Furthermore, this phenomenon can lead to the creation of irregular planetary systems, such as those with grand circumplanetary systems, while the distribution of protoplanet locations may be influenced by the presence of a host star's magnetic field. In the mid-20th century, computer scientists faced a significant challenge: efficiently utilizing limited memory and disk storage for data, especially when performing iterative calculations across large datasets. learning techniques for process analysis and prediction. This approach can be
adapted to other domains and data sets, providing a blueprint for evaluating and
comparing state-of-the-art deep learning models in other research areas.  We
emphasize the significance of combining theoretical research with practical process
mining applications, highlighting this as an open research question. Our research extends previous studies by Cassart et al. and Berthet et al., both focused on truly random graphs, to also consider systems that are not necessarily symmetric. However, when the system is semi-connected and composed of multiple interconnected components, it shares behavioral characteristics with a system that is fully connected in each component. Our methodological approach involves establishing the precise asymptotic properties of systems that are not necessarily symmetric, using theoretical measurements such as the number of equilibrium states and the convergence time. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been observed to fall short when compared to their mesh and image-based counterparts in terms of reliability. This discrepancy is attributed to the irregular nature of point clouds causing traditional robustness measures to be ineffective. To address this challenge, our novel framework called Transformation-Unique Smoothing (TPC) leverages a unique combination of interpolation and normalization techniques to transform point clouds into a more stable form similar to meshes and images. By utilizing this stable representation, our model achieves superior performance in benchmark tests, particularly in evaluating the robustness of models trained with TPC. Furthermore, our model's ability to withstand diverse transformation types ensures optimal performance in real-world scenarios. This innovative approach lays the groundwork for enhancing the robustness of neural network-based point cloud models. Additionally, we introduce a unique evaluation metric called the Smoothing Quality (SQ) score to assess the effectiveness of smoothing point clouds, demonstrating the superiority of TPC over existing methods with comprehensive comparisons, including quantitative analyses, qualitative visual examinations, and indicative case studies. Our model is publicly available for public use at https://github.com/author-name/tpc and has been incorporated into the PyTSM framework. With its exceptional performance, we confidently advocate for the adoption of the transformation-unique smoothing approach over conventional methods. This research paper is a extended version of our previously published paper presented at the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2020) and is now a full-length paper published in the Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) journal. This research paper has also been included in the NeurIPS 2020 (December) Supplement and received the 2020 NeurIPS Citation Diversity Encouragement Award. This award recognizes our commitment to diversity in action by incorporating diverse evaluation criteria, such as the Smoothing Quality (SQ) score, to evaluate the effectiveness of transformation-unique smoothing in point clouds. This achievement has inspired a follow-up investigation into our model's application to mesh models, which has been incorporated into the official PyTSM package. This research has been supported by the National Science Foundation under Grant CNS-1440402, the University of Colorado Boulder, and the University of British Columbia. We would like to extend our gratitude to our model's predecessor, the ResNet50 model, for laying the foundation upon which our novel transformation-unique smoothing approach was built. Temporal knowledge graph completion is an emerging task that aims to predict temporal relationships between entities. Unlike traditional knowledge graph completion, which focuses on static relationships, this task deals with time-specific connection data. A key challenge in TKGC is modeling temporal variability within the graph, with relationships changing over time. We propose a novel, flexible representation that leverages time-specific and time-agnostic representations. Moreover, our approach employs a form of temporal soft clustering, using an adaptive soft temporal superposition (ASTrO) method, to create time-specific representations from time-agnostic ones. ASTrO is based on a low-rank matrix factorization that allows for interpretable results and is independent of existing KGC models. We integrate our representation framework with off-the-shelf graph neural networks, demonstrating the effectiveness of our method on publicly available datasets. Our results reveal that our low-rank, model-agnostic representations yield superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. Moreover, our approach provides transparent, cluster-based results, highlighting the temporal variability within the graph. Furthermore, we observe that our method achieves comparable performance to specialized, high-performance models while employing a more compact model architecture. Our code is publicly available for reproducibility and to facilitate the exploration of TKGCs. Additionally, we introduce an open dataset collection framework, enabling the creation of supplemental data for further TKGC research. The concept of polarization is highly relevant in assessing the credibility of news sources and measuring the influence of fake news on social media. However, measuring polarization poses a significant challenge, primarily due to the absence of standardized normalization procedures. Existing studies often begin research with already normalized polarization data sets, thus hindering a thorough understanding of the complex methods used to analyze these data. This paper focuses on proposing two novel methods for comparing and normalizing polarization networks and graphs. Specifically, it presents two potential solutions for normalizing polarized networks: first, a method for scaling network polarizability relative to its original scale; second, a normalization technique for polarized networks utilizing the maximum and minimum theoretical scores. These methods are applied to 25 prominent news sources across three countries, using both Google's News Index and AlternativeFacts datasets. Our analysis utilizes multiple semantic analysis techniques, combined with citation impact analysis, to demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods normalizing polarized networks. Finally, our methodology is also adaptable to graph-based polarizability analysis, as evident from our examination of European Parliament roll-call vote data. Our approach offers a practical solution for dealing with the methodological shortcomings of previous research, thus paving the way for a more comprehensive exploration of polarized networks and graphs. Furthermore, our methods are publicly available for public use. Additionally, we highlight the potential applications of our methodology to a variety of polarized network datasets, including social media graphs and legislative vote networks. Nonetheless, there are aspects of polarizability that our methods do not fully capture, such as polarized graphs with non-linear structures. Nonetheless, our methods provide a significant step forward in the design and analysis of polarized networks, and we anticipate that they will be useful to many researchers working in this area. Nonetheless, we also recognize that polarizability measures can be susceptible to external influences, such as noise, that can mask a network's true polarized nature, thus we propose a method for filtering out such disturbances, such as, for example, homogeneous opinions within a single node, to gain a more accurate understanding of a network's polarization level. This challenge is illustrated through the analysis of a legislative vote network, involving two variables: the degree of polarization and the amount of noise present. Our results demonstrate that our methods for comparing and normalizing polarized networks, graph-based polarizability analysis, as well as our proposed methods for filtering out disturbances, yield outcomes that align with experts' perceptions and existing research, thus validating the effectiveness of these methods. We introduce HyperPrompt, an innovative architecture that utilizes HyperNetworks to create adaptable task-conditioning for self-attention in Transformers through prompt-based generation. This architecture allows multiple tasks to be learned in an a task-conditioned manner, even when there is no explicit task identification information available. Experiments demonstrate that HyperPrompt outperforms current state-of-the-art models like Prompt-Tuning and Task-C conditioned Transformers in cross-lingual and few-shot learning settings. Furthermore, HyperPrompt shows significant gains over these models when the dataset is limited. We also find that HyperPrompt's HyperPrompt HyperNetwork is capable of selecting optimal task-conditioning through self-prompts, even in the absence of explicit target information. This is a notable finding because it suggests the possibility of a HyperNetwork-based approach for addressing data-free hyperparameter optimization. The source code for HyperPrompt is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrua/HyperPrompt. Additionally, model parameters for the tasks we evaluated are available upon request. We hope this work sparks further research on the integration of HyperNetworks and prompt-based learning to enhance the performance of Transformers in multi-task learning scenarios. Experimental results indicate that HyperPrompt yields superior performance over other models in cross-lingual and few-shot learning settings, showcasing its potential as a state-of-the-art paradigm for testing multi-task learning models. Additionally, HyperPrompt has the benefit of being computationally efficient due to its hyperprompt hypernetwork, which allows it to produce flexible task-conditioning without needing to undergo task-conditioning training. We believe this work is relevant to the NLP community because it may pave the way for the development of more sophisticated multi-task learning models through the integration of HyperNetworks and prompt-based learning. Furthermore, HyperPrompt's ability to optimize task-conditioning without requiring explicit target information may also facilitate the exploration of novel approaches for addressing hyperparameter optimization in deep learning models. The search for rare $\Sigma^+$ baryon decays with leptons, specifically $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, $\Sigma^+ \to \Lambda \mu^+ \mu^-$, and $\Sigma^+ \to \Lambda \mu^+ \mu^- (\Lambda \to p \pi^0)$, has yielded first evidence for a decay mode that does not conform to expectations within the Standard Model. The findings originate from 1.0 ${\text {fb}}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected at 7 and 8 TeV by the LHCb. The observed count for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, with 5.4 standard deviations after accounting for background, significantly exceeds the predicted rate under the Standard Model. The branching fraction for this decay, restricted to an invariant diameter below 0.16 ${\text {GeV}}^2$, is determined as $(2.9 \pm 0.5 \pm 0.3 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{-8}$, with an unitary 90% confidence interval. This result holds the potential to reveal underlying theories if the decay's characteristics do not align with Standard Model expectations. Various new physics models, such as those involving scalar or vector particles and contributions from anomalous $\Sigma^+ \to u\bar{s}$ transitions, can be excluded or placed under scrutiny. Furthermore, limits on branching fractions for $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $\Sigma^+ \to \Lambda \mu^+ \mu^-$ have been established at levels of $2.3 \times 10^{-8}$ and $2.8 \times 10^{-8}$, respectively. Moreover, an upper limit on the $\Sigma^+ \to \Lambda \mu^+ \mu^- (\Lambda \to p \pi^0)$ decay mode, taking into account radiative and non-radiative components, is set at $4.5 \times 10^{-8}$. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Nernst effect in magnetic materials near their magnetic transitions may lead to the development of sensitive magnetic field detectors. However, the underlying mechanisms behind the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials are not yet fully understood and likely involve a combination of the spin-flip and orbit-driven contributions. The orbit-driven contribution is associated with the magnetization transition and the formation of magnetic domains. While extensive research has focused on materials that transition from ferromagnetic to antiferromagnetic states, few studies have examined the Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic materials due to methodological challenges. Our study investigates the Nernst effect in the antiferromagnetic material Mn$_3$NiN, conducted through precise thermal and magnetic control during measurements, and reveals an abnormally large anomalous Nernst coefficient compared to other transition metals. The results indicate that the anomalous Nernst effect in Mn$_3$NiN is governed by the change in magnetic entropy rather than the change in magnetic susceptibility, and we propose that the unusual behavior of the anomalous Nernst coefficient is related to the unique spin canting of the Mn$_3$NiN structure. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that the anomalous Nernst effect can be understood through the free energy model, and we explore the potential of engineering the spin canting of materials with the Nernst effect to develop highly sensitive magnetic field detectors. Our study also highlights the suitability of the heavy metal interface as a key component for such devices. Additionally, we observe an unusual non-linear resistance change in the temperature and magnetic field dependence, and we propose that these non-linear responses may enable the development of sensitive magnetic field detectors that can be operated at room temperature. Our study demonstrates the value of investigating the Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic materials and highlights the potential of the Mn$_3$NiN structure as a starting point for the design of highly sensitive magnetic field detectors. Teachers assign tasks to students and provide feedback in the form of labels, which are usually multiple choice based on the teacher's expertise. Having multiple teachers instruct the same student allows for more comprehensive feedback, but also results in a larger label set that is costly to procure. In this paper, we introduce the concept of multi-instructor labeled data and focus on the label redistribution problem, where the aim is to retrain the model using a more cost-effective subset of labels chosen by the instructor with the highest confidence, subject to a diversity constraint. We propose the multi-instructor labeled subset selection problem and develop an integrated framework that chooses the subset of labels and redistributes the confidence of the instructors, based on a model-agnostic diversity metric that ensures diversity satisfaction. For computational efficiency, we introduce a pairwise iterative logits ensemble algorithm that converges to a locally optimal solution. Experimental evaluations on three large-scale datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in improving model performance, achieving significant gains over baseline models, with an average improvement of 8.28%. The proposed method also outperforms other label ensemble methods, and shows particular advantage in datasets with a large number of instructors. The implementation of our method is publicly available at https://github.com/zwang84/pile. With the rapid growth of annotated datasets labeled by multiple instructors, our results demonstrate the potential of our framework to enhance model performance in these datasets. Furthermore, our method can also be applied to other ensemble learning scenarios that involve both agreement and competition. In such scenarios, the model learns to focus on the most confident and diverse labels, resulting in improved performance. With the current trend of large-scale datasets being annotated by numerous instructors, our method provides a way to prioritize and combine these labels, and our results demonstrate a notable average improvement of 8.28% over baseline models. With the proliferation of crowdsourcing and multi-instructor labeling, our method is expected to become a vital tool for promoting cost-effective, high-quality data annotation practices. In addition to its numerical evaluation, the project's repository includes an interactive visualization module that showcases the confidence values and diversity scores of the instructors, as well as the selected labels, using a variety of layouts and themes. With its efficient implementation and user-friendly interface, the project has the potential to become a leading framework for addressing the multi-instructor labeled data label redistribution problem, and may also be adapted to other ensemble learning scenarios. Understanding and manipulating materials at the atomic level requires significant control and precision. This paper discusses the improvements made to oxidanomalous point defect engineering in 2D materials through resonance tunneling of an oxygen atom row. By manipulating oxygen atom placement, researchers achieved a 200-fold increase in accuracy over traditional methods. Additionally, this approach allows for the detection of subtle interactions between point defects and surrounding lattice structures, enhancing the accuracy of defect positioning. A key challenge in working with complex multivariate time series data is to identify the causal relationships within the system. This task, known as causal discovery, has far-reaching applications in fields like finance, economics, and medicine. Existing methods for causal discovery typically rely on a single static snapshot of the data and assume a stationary system. In reality, systems often evolve dynamically, and systems typically require a continuous stream of data to maintain their structure. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel algorithm called Deep Dynamic Eco (Causal Structure Discovery). Eco (ECO) is a connection estimation operator that discovers a dynamic graph describing the system's current structure and its evolution over time. Built on top of this foundation, we propose Deep Eco (DECOD), a deep learning-based model that can process continuous multivariate time series data. By leveraging the Deep Eco framework, we explore case studies on artificial and real-world datasets, highlighting its performance and cost benefits over traditional methods. The code for Deep Eco is openly available on GitHub (https://github.com/QuantNetwork/Deep-Eco). In line with standard practice, we utilize publicly accessible datasets obtained from sources such as the M4 Competition, the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), the Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), and the Python libraries PyTorch and Scipy. In our research, we demonstrate the capability of Deep Eco to accurately predict complex behavioral patterns in economic and financial systems from multivariate time series data. Furthermore, we investigate the potential of Deep Eco to serve as a proactive alert system, leveraging its ability to continuously analyze real-time data and predict future system breakdowns in conjunction with its static and dynamic graph components. The underlying Causal Structure Discovery algorithm within Deep Eco enables the exploration of underlying driver factors associated with such predictions. As a result, this model holds great promise for its application in monitoring the stability of complex economic and financial systems. A cell's behavior during dispersal and movement is influenced by various mechanisms such as cell body contraction, adhesive forces to the surrounding substrate, and chemical signals. These mechanisms can provoke significant changes in cell shape, causing parts of the cell to stretch out into extended structures like filopodia or rich networks of branching fibers. The lipid membranes that make up these extensions can also undergo independent movement. Our model builds upon existing kinetic exchange theory and incorporates reactions that occur on membrane surfaces that are moving independently. It maintains the typical mean-field approximations used in T1 dynamics models, based on the model developed in [SSK20]. Our model can be applied to describe the distribution of proteins within cells migrating over a surface, influenced by chemical signals, and can also handle branching fiber networks. Additionally, we provide numerical solutions to the resulting system of PDEs using a hybrid front-tracking/FEM method. Our results demonstrate that chemical signals can have a notable impact on the migration of cells and the distribution of proteins within them. Our model is relevant to past research [SSK20] studying the migration of single cells and can be extended to model the behavior of cells in response to chemical signals in heterogeneous networks. Our model is currently being developed for use with the software package Dune[URL], with the source code available upon request. Initially, a machine learning model is applied to identify suspicious addresses based on transaction behavior. Subsequently, currency trails connected to these suspicious addresses are characterized and the factors influencing trail length are analyzed. Our findings indicate that a combination of cryptographic hash functions and network architecture contributes to the limited length of currency trails. In response, a novel 'TraceBack' algorithm is developed to enhance detection capabilities of currency trails. Through successful implementations and evaluations, TraceBack demonstrates its effectiveness in identifying currency trails with a low error rate. The developed approach is adaptable to multiple cryptocurrency networks, as evidenced by our experimental results. The study finds that quantum leap metrology yields the most accurate measurements, but also reveals that this approach can be simulated using a single cavity and a reflectivity parameter, effectively demonstrating the equivalence between the two-cavity system and its single-cavity representation. The study further shows that quantum leap metrology can achieve an exponential improvement in accuracy, specifically an $e^{N}$-scale improvement, where N represents the number of photons in the system. The study also highlights the challenges and potential applications of quantum leap metrology, but also notes the possibility of implementing this strategy using a single cavity and a variety of unitary transformations. The study concludes by suggesting that quantum leap metrology may offer a more scalable and robust approach to achieving super-Poisson photon statistics in cavity QED systems. Nonetheless, our analysis reveals that variable network efficiency within these systems can substantially impact performance and scalability when applications are running across multiple vendors. Furthermore, we identify the existing measurement methods as inadequate, prompting us to introduce a new method for assessing application scalability, as well as propose a set of benchmarks for evaluating network clouds. Through our study, we demonstrate that cloud providers' strategies can result in network elasticity limitations, leading to decreased performance and scalability when applying multi-vendor deployments. In response, we present enhanced strategies for system design, along with a prototype, to mitigate the effects of network elasticity variability and achieve superior scalability and performance in multi-vendor settings. Overall, our research underlines the significance of network elasticity in cloud systems and suggests it should be treated as a critical design consideration. Finally, we believe our findings and solutions can also apply to other complex systems that rely on networks with variable elasticity. In the case of network clouds, we propose a set of design principles that prioritize flexibility and future-proofing, advocating for the adoption of resilient applications that can effectively utilize available bandwidth and facilitate collaborative behavior between systems. Finally, we anticipate this work to contribute positively to the ongoing development of cloud computing and our community. Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle. Especially in scenarios where context dimensions are substantial. This paper addresses a decentralized, memoryless contextual linear bandit learning problem. In this problem, agents that observe the context and make decisions are physically isolated from the learner. This learner executes the learning process but remains unaware of the context. Contexts are assumed to be generated randomly and are observable to the agents. Our objective is to maximize cumulative rewards while minimizing communication between the learner and the agents. To achieve this, we develop two communication-efficient policies. These policies are free from assumptions about the communication channel or the distribution of the context. Notably, one of these policies relies on a limited binary signal and significantly reduces communication costs. We establish near-optimal performance guarantees for both proposed policies. These guarantees hold in expectation and are based on the actual observed data. Moreover, we provide a comparison of our approaches with existing solutions. This comparison highlights the advantages of our methods over existing solutions. It is worth noting that existing solution references are mostly based on existing results from the full-information learning domain. Our solution addresses a significant gap in the bandits learning domain. Finally, we complement our theoretical results with a practical demonstration of our methods. This demonstration shows positive results on a real-world application. This application involves decoding contextual video descriptions over limited communication links. Our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our learning algorithms in this setting. This effectiveness translates to significant improvements in video quality. These improvements result from the reduced communication costs enabled by our learning algorithms. As a result, these algorithms enable the encoding of more visual details. These details are crucial for understanding video content. Our results indicate that our approaches outperform the existing state-of-the-art methods. Especially, our proposed policy that employs a binary signal performs better than existing solutions. This performance gain results from its ability to leverage the knowledge of the distribution of the context. This knowledge is utilized to generate an optimal binary signal. This signal is generated based on the actual data and maximizes the logarithm of the probability of the context. This logarithm is a component of the expected cumulative reward. Our results demonstrate that this binary signal has a lower dimension than the contextual linear bandits state-of-the-art solution. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the slow nature of fluid flow, fluid particle interactions are typically modeled using large time steps, but this approach can lead to unrealistic particle collision times. To address this issue, we developed a new method based on the integration of relative particle movement during collisions, leveraging the principle of conservation of momentum. As a result, we can utilize smaller time steps for capturing collision dynamics and map them onto large simulation time steps. A numerical simulation was conducted to validate our method, and the proposed technique was compared to existing models. Our study reveals that the standard model overestimates collision duration, while the model incorporating friction overcorrects this, yet still poses numerical stability issues. Conversely, our proposed method delivers accurate collision duration without impacting the stability of simulation, and with significantly smaller time steps, allowing for more precise simulation results. Additionally, we observed that our method can facilitate the implementation of external forces during collisions. Our proposed method demonstrates superior results compared to existing models, particularly in simulations involving a wide range of particle sizes. As such, this method holds the potential to be integrated with other simulation techniques, such as DEM-SPH, for more precise simulation of particle flows. To further validate our method, simulations were conducted under different time steps, revealing that our method can accurately capture collision dynamics even with very large time steps. Despite being ubiquitous, negation poses significant challenges to modern natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering English reading comprehension dataset. It demands that models infer the implications of negated statements within passages, collected from a diverse set of paragraphs featuring varied negation cues. Additionally, human evaluators asked questions regarding the implications of these negations and performed a series of challenging tasks: paraphrasing negated statements, altering the scope of negation, and reversing the negation, resulting in distinct groups of question-answer pairs that current models struggle to tackle without resorting to workarounds. Our CONDAQA dataset comprises 14,182 challenging question-answer pairs, encompassing over 200 unique negation cues and proves particularly demanding for leading NLP models. Notably, even the best-performing model (UnifiedQA-v2-3b) managed only 42% accuracy according to our consistency metric, significantly lagging behind the 81% achieved by human evaluators. In a bid to fuel further NLP innovations, we publicly release our dataset, along with comprehensive evaluations involving fully-finetuned, few-shot, and zero-shot scenarios. Our CONDAQA dataset is expected to drive the development of more sophisticated, negation-aware NLP models that can tackle complex language understanding tasks. Its diverse nature and challenging protocols make it an ideal platform for evaluating the progress made by such models. Its model architecture combines a negation-aware attention mechanism with a novel contrastive learning approach that recognizes the implicit positive counterparts of negatively phrased statements. The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) is equipped with a highly sophisticated first-level jet trigger system, which has been instrumental in identifying crucial events containing jets since the start of heavy ion and proton-proton collisions in 2009. This system, based on the ATLAS custom-designed Very High Speed Trigger readout control system (VLSI), has undergone significant upgrades to keep pace with the LHC's escalating luminosity and data rates. Initially designed to handle 1 pb-1 of data per second, the system now handles 40 pb-1 of data per second in the Heavy Ion mode and 1 fb-1 of data per second in the Proton-proton mode. To support this increased capacity, a new full-scale production board called FPGAboard ULTRA has been developed, featuring an Advanced Telephony RISC Core (ATRC) and four custom-designed custom Digital Signal Processing (DSP) engines. This board utilizes an Ultrascale+ FPGA and is part of the ATLAS jet trigger system's central module known as the Central Jet Trigger (CJT). It replaces the legacy VLSI-based CJC module, providing improved performance and reduced power consumption. The CJC module combines data from the ATLAS calorimeter system and makes decisions at the 40 MHz pulse rate before delivering decisions to the ATLAS high-level trigger system at a 1 kHz rate for further analysis. The CJC module consists of eight independent jet finding paths, with each path capable of processing 32, 64, or 128 jet findings based on predefined thresholds. The FPGAboard ULTRA has undergone extensive testing, and it has been successfully integrated into the ATLAS jet trigger system as part of the LHC's Upgrade I, with the first prototype board having been operated during Run-2 of the LHC. The board's design and its performance testing are discussed in this paper. The board features a 12Gb 32-bit double-data-rate third-generation Memory Interface (MI-3) memory interface with a 4800-bit-per-second data transfer capacity. The board's digital signal processing engines have been optimized for finding up to 64 jets with an energy threshold of 0.2 GeV at the 40 MHz pulse rate. The board's design provides improved performance, reduced power consumption, and higher jet finding capacity compared to its legacy counterpart. The board has achieved outstanding performance results during Run-2 and the current Run-3 of the LHC, delivering an exceptionally high jet finding capacity

The formation of spiral structure in a galaxy is thought to result from the interaction between its rotating flat disc and central bar components. Recent observations of nearby galaxies have made it possible to measure the pitch angles of their spiral patterns. These measurements can be compared with a theoretical model that utilizes a galactic coordinate system. The model incorporates a bar within the galaxy's disc and calculates the local pitch angle at different radial distances. It demonstrates that the relationship between the pitch angle and radial distance forms a straight line when plotted in a specific coordinate system. The model also provides a method for determining the natural frequency of a galaxy's density waves. When applied to the Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies, this model predicts that their natural frequency would match that of an 11-arm pattern. It suggests that the Milky Way has a radial density that follows a $R^{1.4}$ distribution and that the natural frequency of its bar component is greater than that of its spiral arms. The model can be used to create design patterns for galaxy simulations, potentially improving their stability. It includes a feature that prevents the development of unstable modes within these simulations. Furthermore, this study reveals that magnetic fields have a lesser impact on mergers with less abundant gas, resulting in only slight changes to the shape and temperature of disks, presenting a scenario for distinguishing observations. A notable consequence of this research is the suggestion that magnetic fields play a crucial role in shaping the morphology of galaxy mergers, especially those with abundant gas, and that they could significantly enhance the diversity of merger patterns. The connection between the pion's matrix elements and lattice gauge theory two-point and light-by-light scattering functions is clarified. This involves converting the well-studied two-point and scattering problems into a linear diagonalization problem. I demonstrate that the often-used Isgur-Wambach relation, which relates the pion's charge radius to its decay constant, can be reinterpreted in this new context. Furthermore, gauge field simulations can be used to model the influence of heavy quark symmetry. These findings provide a clear path forward for the lattice determination of the pion's light-cone distribution function. Specifically, the normally complex task of distributing two currents within the pion can be achieved through a combination of lattice calculations and the diagonalization of a matrix constructed from two-point and light-by-light scattering functions. This approach is universally applicable to any system with quark-antiquark bound states. The proposed method is applicable not only to the pion but also to other mesons, such as charmed and bottometed mesons. The feasibility of the approach is illustrated by estimating the influence of heavy quark symmetry and the associated mass dependence for the lambda baryon. The method is relevant for current and upcoming lattice simulations with precise physical parameters. The proposed approach provides a new perspective on the interpretation of lattice data and simulations in the context of quark structure studies. The methodology is being used to reinterpret existing lattice simulation results for the pion's distribution function and to guide new simulations that will be carried out at the lattice simulation collaboration LHCb. The results from these simulations will be incorporated into the global analysis of pion distribution functions as part of the THQ analysis package. The THQ analysis package combines experimental and theoretical data and is used to determine the non-perturbative quark distribution functions within protons and neutrons. The distribution functions are typically characterized by up to 10 parameters that describe the behavior of a parton at different virtualities. The THQ analysis package will be used to determine these distribution functions at a 2-GeV scale, which is the scale at which quarks within protons and neutrons start behaving non-perturbatively. The results from the lattice simulation will be used to determine the quark condensate at a 0.2-GeV scale, which is relevant for the mass of light quarks. The method will also be used to investigate the role of twist-2 and twist-4 contributions in light-by-light scattering and to determine the relevant parameters for gauge boson distribution functions.

Certain nonlocal phenomena, such as single-particle steering and the EPR paradox, arise due to the particle's entanglement with itself from its initial state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that certain nonlocal phenomena associated with entangled particles, such as boat-parachute systems, can also be explained by the particle's self-entanglement. Consequently, we propose that observing nonlocal effects between two separate points as inherently connected ('entangled') is an inaccurate view and can be seen as a manifestation of the system's self-entanglement. Finally, based on the analysis of a specific scenario involving a spinning dice, we show that the particle's steering is maximized when its state of motion is optimized, which results in a nonlocal effect achieved through classical means. This finding implies that nonlocal effects based on scalar fields can also be achieved classically. Lastly, we suggest that the term "entanglement" be reserved for a scenario where a system becomes connected to itself due to its non-interacting interactions with different environments, as this results in a system state that can't be described locally. Conversely, systems that have only experienced shared environments but haven't become connected to themselves shouldn't be described as entangled. Additionally, we propose the use of the term "strongly correlated" to describe systems that have interacted with each other, as this captures the essence of their correlation without implying a connection to themselves. Finally, we suggest that the term "correlation" be applied broadly to cover all situations where the system's state can't be described locally. Furthermore, we outline a set of loosely related notes on the topic of nonlocal phenomena. Our study provides a detailed overview of identified particle production within the ALICE experiment for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV. Secondary beams such as pions, kaons, (anti-)protons, and $\phi$ mesons have been examined across a broad range of transverse momentum (0.3 to 5.0 GeV/$c$) and centralities. Compared to Pb-Pb collisions, lower particle yields are observed for zero to four proton and lambda production, as well as for phi meson production within the medium and high momentum ranges. At intermediate momenta (2 to 3 GeV/$c$), production of protons and lambda particles exhibits similar results to Pb-Pb collisions. A comparison of the spectra with 0-5% and 40-50% centralities reveals an increase in identified particle production within the most central collisions. Additionally, the calibration of the ALICE central barrel with a newly developed multiplicity-weighted method reflects the characteristics of heavy-ion collisions at the LHC. A comprehensive set of flow coefficients ($v_2$ to $v_4$) is also provided as a function of transverse momentum, centrality, and particle type. Observations from this study, particularly regarding proton and lambda particle results, reveal interesting patterns in the dependence of flow coefficients on particle type. A combined analysis with previous research does not yield a clear understanding of the origin of these trends. Further investigation is advised with increased precision and relevant controls. This study investigates the numerical resolution of a problem that involves completing missing data in Maxwell's equations based on boundary value information, with the aim of recovering an original electric field. A key approach to solving this problem analytically is the quasi-reversibility method, which modifies the original problem to create a globally defined and compact problem for finding the missing data. The method relies on a variational formulation with a Tikhonov regularization term, which is successfully discretized using the finite element method. The recovery of the original electric field field is then achieved through the application of Brezis-Gallouet-Lin's result, yielding a nonlinear system solvable via Newton's method. This research supplies semi-supervised Convolutive NMF, a factorization technique, with previously recorded audio along with sparse features representing musical notes. The goal is to generate a flexible representation of note patterns in an unknown context. When combined with limited annotated data, semi-supervised Convolutive NMF significantly improves the accuracy of note transcriptions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a virtual keyboard simulation and real-world recordings of a piano, applying constraints unique to musical notes to enhance model performance. Compared to alternative methods, semi-supervised Convolutive NMF delivers superior results on both simulated and actual audio. The technique's versatility is also showcased through its application to an historical organ, using a novel keyboard representation and a unique set of annotated data. Furthermore, semi-supervised Convolutive NMF is shown to achieve comparable transcription quality with a conventional keyboard transcription system, both in terms of precision and recall. The method’s potential for reducing the amount of annotated data required is also illustrated. The technique and annotated data used in this research are both made available for public access. Additionally, a comparison with a state-of-the-art musical note transcription model, Mask R-CNN, is included. Although this model surpasses semi-supervised Convolutive NMF in note transcription accuracy, it demands substantial amounts of annotated data and possesses a level of complexity not yet matched by factorization techniques. Nonetheless, semi-supervised Convolutive NMF remains a viable option for low-complexity note transcription systems. Furthermore, due to its efficiency, it continues to be an attractive choice for systems involving real-time note transcription. In such contexts, even slightly lower transcription accuracy in exchange for significantly reduced annotation costs, continues to make semi-supervised Convolutive NMF a preferable solution. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This new approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. This includes individual masses, specific angular momentum, and entropy levels. 

As a key departure from earlier methodologies, the angular velocity distribution within each fluid element may vary. This is different from the traditional approach, where the angular velocity is treated as a global, uniform property of the star. Instead, we solve for the angular velocity in each fluid element through the use of an iterative algorithm. This leads to more precise and adaptable solutions, especially in stars with complex rotation patterns. 

Our implementation utilizes a radially ordered grid to facilitate the solution process, where the position of each fluid element is determined by solving balance equations and calculating Lagrangian derivatives. We have successfully validated our model by replicating the findings of earlier researchers and have employed it to investigate the impact of rotation on supernova collapse and on neutron star formation. This research investigates how Rossby wave vortices influence the behavior of water waves in an infinite, one-dimensional domain, considering both weak and strong vortex conditions. We demonstrate that, in the presence of a strong, long-wavelength vortex, water waves can be described by a modified Hamiltonian Dysthe equation. Conversely, in the case of a weak vortex, a higher-order Dysthe equation applies. Our analysis is valid for waves with moderate amplitudes and frequencies close to the linear frequency. Additionally, we find that the new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation for strong vortices yields more stable solutions than its non-conservative counterpart. Our model is applicable to waves with small to moderate steepness, and we observe that both weak and strong vortex models produce similar results for water waves in the absence of a vortex. This study provides a conservative formulation for the Dysthe equation, which is widely used to model water waves, and highlights the importance of considering circulation when studying deep-water wave behavior. Furthermore, we outline the potential for extending this research to account for water waves in a channel with variable depth. This work is a continuation of our previous finding presented at the 2019 IUTAM Symposium, and we have made this related work openly available in the interest of scientific transparency. In the case of a strong vortex, we have addressed an issue with breathers and have provided a new solution for water waves. This research involves a leading expert in water wave theory, and we have jointly developed and validated the results with an independent numerical approach.
