We propose a new navigation method utilizing a novel graph representation called HiTMap, a hierarchical topological map that facilitates efficient planning and motor control. HiTMap is a two-layered structure comprising a high-level graph representing environment topology and a set of corresponding low-level velocity control maps that guide the robot's movement between connected areas. We integrate HiTMap with dynamic feedback control and online resampling mechanisms to ensure the representation's accuracy and completeness. Our simulation results demonstrate that HiTMap-based navigation outperforms traditional methods, particularly in densely filled environments and with multiple peaks, and the associated code is freely available for public use. Furthermore, we discuss the potential applications and future developments of HiTMap in motion planning. Additionally, we introduce an interactive 3D tool, also available for download, that enables users to create and visualize HiTMap representations. This representation's uniqueness lies in its combination of local detail preservation and global structure, making it an attractive approach for robotic navigation scenarios. Specifically, we examine how the magnetothermal effect can be induced in TMDs when they are brought into proximity with a ferromagnetic substrate. Our theoretical model reveals that the proximity-induced spin-polarized magnetothermal effect arises due to the differential response of spin-up and spin-down electrons to temperature changes under the influence of a nearby magnetic field. Notably, this resulting thermomagnetic torque within the TMD can be controlled through adjustments to the strength of the nearby magnetic field. Object-based programming on GPUs is complicated by the lack of built-in memory management support, which most programming languages provide.  Current solutions involve manual memory management, which can be error-prone and hinder code portability. To address this limitation, this paper introduces DynaSOAr, a novel memory allocator designed for object-based programming on GPUs.  DynaSOAr is a dynamic, object-oriented memory allocator that utilizes a binary tree data structure to efficiently manage memory blocks of any size.  It allows for the creation of objects of any size within user-specified bounds, preventing memory fragmentation caused by objects of irregular sizes.  It also minimizes memory waste through a memory-packed object allocation policy, which aligns objects according to the requirements of GPU memory access, which is highly aligned.  DynaSOAr is a high-performance allocator that uses multiple threads to manage memory blocks, promoting concurrency and efficiency.  It is compatible with CUDA and compatible with OpenCL.  Through extensive benchmarking, DynaSOAr demonstrates significant performance improvements over other memory management methods, including a binary allocator called BinSOAr and a flat allocator called FlatSOAr, particularly in applications with high object creation rates and complex data structures.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr offers a level of memory safety that is unmatched by other memory allocators, including BinSOAr and FlatSOAr, due to its bound checking feature, which prevents memory breaches and crashes.  Additionally, DynaSOAr facilitates code portability by providing a standardized memory management interface, allowing programmers to write device functions that are both efficient and reliable.  In conclusion, DynaSOAr presents a cutting-edge memory allocator that solves the memory management problems associated with object-based programming on GPUs, while also offering high performance, memory safety, and code portability.  It serves as a model for the design of memory allocators for object-based programming on GPUs, combining the principles of object-oriented programming, efficiency, and safety. Music navigation on audio streams with minimal user interaction relies heavily on advanced machine learning algorithms. Despite significant advancements in modeling user behavior, developing scalable models for real-time music playback remains a persistent challenge. One key obstacle hindering progress is the lack of large-scale, high-quality datasets containing user ratings for popular music genres. To address this issue, we've introduced the Pied Piper Dataset, which incorporates user preferences collected via the Meta Quest platform. Utilizing a dataset of over 21,000 ratings from over 10,000 users covering 377 genres, we conducted comprehensive evaluations of multiple implicit feedback models. Our experiments demonstrated that neural network-based models outperform traditional methods, with significant improvements in model efficiency and accuracy. We also explored model interpretability and discovered notable insights regarding user behavior, including preferences for exploring genres over creating long playlists and a strong desire for discovering new music. Our findings, coupled with the Pied Piper Dataset, have the potential to drive innovations in music recommendation, playback, and discovery. We openly share the dataset, available at https://piedpiperdataset.org/, in the hopes that it will inspire future advancements in the field. We strongly believe that it will continue to fuel significant breakthroughs in music recommendation over the years to come. The dataset's accompanying evaluation framework, implicit feedback tools, and experimental setup have also been openly contributed to the community, along with the dataset itself. We've detailed the dataset's creation process, evaluation methodologies, and key results in the paper available at the Pied Piper Dataset website (https://piedpiperdataset.org/). The expression "translation" holds a diverse range of meanings, encompassing various concepts such as cultural, linguistic, and software interpretations. In the field of software development, translation can represent the process of adapting existing technologies to meet new technological standards, or redefining the underlying principles of a technology to align them with our current understanding. This thesis explores how the translation of grid computing concepts into practical applications influenced the field's development and eventual shift in terminology to cloud computing. Through an in-depth analysis of historical data and primary accounts from key figures, the study reveals the transformative impact of translating grid computing into a practical reality. In response to an interview question, the study's participant noted that the term "cloud" served as a form of translation, facilitating a deeper understanding of complex distributed systems by comparing them to familiar analogies, such as mist or fog. This finding prompts consideration of how the translation of innovative technologies into tangible forms affects both their development and eventual adoption. Furthermore, it is proposed that a transformational approach, involving a deeper examination and refinement of a technology's underlying principles, is a crucial aspect of technological progress. Additionally, the study highlights the value of adopting a transdisciplinary approach that draws from the many interpretations of translation, applying its various concepts to better comprehend the complex processes involved in software development. Through its exploration of the evolution of grid computing and cloud computing, the study provides valuable insights that can be applied to other areas of innovative technology development. Ultimately, it is hoped that this research will contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the development and adoption of complex technologies, as well as the essential role that translation, in all its forms, plays in these processes. This thesis concludes by presenting several avenues for further research, centered on the investigation of other technologies through a translation lens, as well as the development of a more comprehensive theoretical framework for understanding the translation process. This framework, referred to as TST, can be applied across multiple areas of innovative technology development, and is anticipated to facilitate a more in-depth examination of both the development and adoption of cloud computing, as well as its underlying components, such as virtualization and service-oriented architecture. Additionally, TST is designed to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the complex processes involved in software development, as well as a more effective approach to predicting and addressing the challenges that arise during the translation process. Furthermore, this thesis proposes that TST can be applied to other technologies, such as big data and the Internet of Things, as well as to the development of new technologies, such as quantum computing. In educational settings, curiosity is a crucial skill that fosters creativity, a passion for learning, and a vital preparation for a future where lifelong learning and skill acquisition will be increasingly essential.  Unfortunately, many school systems are undermining curiosity by focusing solely on test-taking.  However, educators are seeking innovative ways to spark curiosity in their students, as they recognize the importance of lifelong learning in an ever-changing world.  One promising approach is the integration of artificial intelligence into educational experiences that are both highly interactive and tailored to individual students.  However, the challenge lies in developing an effective measure of curiosity in these complex, technology-driven learning environments.  Existing measures of curiosity typically focus on individual learners, using self-reporting surveys that fail to capture the dynamics of curiosity within groups.  Furthermore, these measures often ignore the role of external stimuli in fueling curiosity.  To address these limitations, we propose a novel, multi-faceted method for assessing curiosity in group learning settings, combining data from verbal and non-verbal behaviors, physiological responses, and performance.  This approach allows for curiosity to be evaluated dynamically throughout a learning experience.  We validated our approach through a real-world application, involving 32 middle-school students in a programming course.  Our results demonstrated a strong correlation between our curiosity metrics and a control group consisting of student self-assessments, while also highlighting the differences in group curiosity dynamics.  Our research provides a foundation for educators and developers to design more engaging, curious, and effective learners.  Additionally, our approach can be integrated into various subjects and age groups, offering a groundbreaking way to understand curiosity in group learning contexts.  Our findings also shed light on group curiosity dynamics, potentially informing theories on social learning and group behavior.  To facilitate replication and further development, we have made our method publicly available and are inviting the research community to build upon our work.  As artificial intelligence-driven learning experiences become the norm, our approach may serve as a model for evaluating curiosity in an increasingly important area.  To answer these pressing educational questions, we recommend investigating learning environments powered by artificial intelligence that are capable of detecting and stimulating curiosity in real-time.  Our recommendation is being considered by the provider of the programming platform used in our study, resulting in enhanced features that recognize individual students' curiosity levels and adapt the learning experience accordingly.  However, more research is needed to fully understand the implications of these developments on the learning process.  As a result, we propose the creation of an open-source community around our approach, to accelerate the exploration

A connected graph G is considered traceable if there exists a Hamiltonian path that visits every vertex exactly once. We explored the property of being traceable in repeated line graphs, specifically examining how the number of 2-factor cycles in a graph relates to this property. Our findings include a characterization for the repeated line graphs of cubic trees and certain families of cubic graphs. We also provide lower and upper estimates for the hamiltonian path index of these graphs, demonstrating that this index can vary significantly depending on the choice of path. Additionally, we identified a set of quadruplets of hamiltonian paths with distinct lengths that exist within the repeated line graph of a specific cubic tree. This work builds upon previous research by Garcia, Goyal, and Marquez, who investigated the relationship between hamiltonian paths and 2-factor cycles in line graphs. We extend this research to repeated line graphs and offer upper and lower estimates for the hamiltonian path index of these graphs. A key aspect of this work involves a novel application of the graph's hamiltonian property, which enables the determination of a hamiltonian path once a specific cycle is identified within the graph. This paper introduces a new validation tool for Tezos smart contracts, called HELMHOLTZ, which utilizes refinement types to ensure contracts meet predetermined security criteria. Developed in cooperation with Tezos stakeholders and contract developers, HELMHOLTZ leverages the Coq proof assistant and Zeilenauch's type-checking functionality to verify the soundness of contracts at the Michelson level. By combining refinement types with the contract's operational semantics, HELMHOLTZ establishes a link between safe types and the Michelson Virtual Machine's refactoring of expressions, known as the Uncluttering process. This connection enables validators to identify potentially hazardous code patterns, such as infinite loops and unauthorized resource access, even in cases where the type checker for Michelson fails to detect errors. To illustrate HELMHOLTZ's effectiveness, we present a series of examples, including a real-world contract previously deployed on the Tezos network, which the tool successfully identifies as insecure. To overcome the type checker's limitations, users can either modify the type annotations or refactor the code to prevent the original type checker from checking correctly. In response to these changes, HELMHOLTZ determines if the revised contract is now free from errors and suitable for deployment on the Tezos network. Additionally, HELMHOLTZ provides a user-friendly interface for users to express security requirements with refinement types, ensuring the tool's user-friendliness and efficiency. Furthermore, we explore potential extensions for user-defined error handlers within the Tezos environment. With a growing community around static contract verification, this research aims to contribute significantly to the secure development of smart contracts for the Tezos blockchain. To facilitate replication and further advancement of this research, we have made the proofs, implementations, and validation configurations openly available for review and improvement. In the current version, HELMHOLTZ focuses exclusively on contract deployment, ignoring contract migration functionality. As the field of smart contract verification continues to evolve, so too will our validation tool, with future developments to be publicly disclosed in subsequent versions. Furthermore, we invite all parties to collaborate and contribute to HELMHOLTZ's development and refinement types-based validation methodology. In the interest of full transparency and openness, we invite referees and community members to provide feedback and suggestions for enhancement, which we will incorporate and adapt in the tool's future iterations. With this collaborative approach, we aim to establish a joint effort to promote secure smart contract development within the Tezos ecosystem. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This paper introduces an intermediate representation called "logical pseudocodes," which bridge the gap between these domains. By applying a formal specification to logical pseudocodes, we can translate them into proofs in natural deduction. Conversely, we can generate logical pseudocodes from natural deduction proofs. This duality enables us to analyze algorithms through the lens of logical pseudocodes and natural deduction proofs, offering a more comprehensive understanding of their behavior. We demonstrate this framework with a simple imperative algorithm and show that it facilitates modular specification and verification. Additionally, we discuss the potential for using logical pseudocodes to identify useful connections between programming, logic, and mathematics. Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance at a relatively low computational cost. A key method in this area, the unsupervised cycleGAN approach, has demonstrated great promise in restoring standard-dose CT images from low-dose CT images without requiring paired training data. However, the use of two neural network generators in the training process is a significant limitation, primarily because the extra generator adds complexity and memory demands. In response to these issues, we have introduced a new cycleGAN method based on a single, switchable generator. By incorporating adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) layers, this generator can efficiently produce both low-dose to standard-dose CT and standard-dose to low-dose CT transformations during training. The results of our evaluations, conducted using two publicly available CT datasets, demonstrate that our proposed method not only matches the performance of the baseline cycleGAN method using two generators but also significantly outperforms it. Moreover, our experiments involving quantitative evaluation and visual assessment show that our method produces restorations with enhanced resolution and contrast, producing restorations that are not only subjectively better but also objectively better than those generated using the baseline method. The code for our model has been made available on the GitHub platform. Our research indicates that the switchable generator strategy offers a viable alternative to the dual-generator approach used in previous cycleGAN applications, and we anticipate that this method will be adopted in various image transformation tasks. Furthermore, we have investigated the influence of the AdaIN switchable strategy on image restoration using a separate dataset, with surprising findings that the method's effectiveness is resolution-independent. Our exploration into these findings has yielded valuable insights that can be applied to future research in the field. In conclusion, our innovative AdaIN-Switchable cycleGAN model has set a new performance benchmark for low-dose CT image restoration, and we are confident that this research will pave the way for breakthroughs in other image enhancement challenges. This model incorporates a novel contrastive learning technique that utilizes unlabelled dialog data to capture the implicit structural information present in dialog datasets. Moreover, our analysis on the dialog dataset obtained through online crowdsourcing revealed that the majority of the datasets contain underlying tree structures, thereby demonstrating the effectiveness and relevance of the proposed SPACE-2 approach. In multi-task reinforcement learning, sharing knowledge across tasks can significantly improve learning efficiency. However, the challenge also arises in preventing the phenomenon of catastrophic interference, which hinders the learning process by eliminating previously acquired skills. In our research, we introduce a novel modular approach to multi-task reinforcement learning by segregating task representations. We demonstrate in a range of experiments that this approach outperforms alternative methods, especially in complex scenarios, In our experiments, we utilized the Multi-Task DeepCOPO to evaluate our modular approach. We conducted a series of experiments to test the benefits of our model, including a simple discrete task, a set of random MRP tasks, and more complex continuous control tasks with latent task identities. The results show that the modular approach delivers enhanced performance when comparing policy performance, the number of episodes required to converge, and the test performance. Furthermore, the analysis of the heatmaps representing the value functions in the easy discrete task and the latent variable control task also illustrates the modular approach's capacity to maintain separate task representations. In contrast, the unified baseline policy failed to converge in half of the runs for the easy discrete task and the random MRP tasks, and the learned policies suffered from catastrophic interference, resulting in poor performance on previously learned tasks. Additionally, the data also suggests that the modular approach avoids interference by separating task representations in the easy discrete task. Moreover, the results from the continuous control tasks with latent task identities indicate that the modular approach delivers significant improvements over the baseline policy when multiple skills are required to solve a problem, resulting in a 450% increase in performance in one of the cases. The code for our experiments has been made available online for public access. In our research, we also explored a range of related questions, including how to select the tasks to be shared, and the design of modular networks by maximizing shared and unique action-value functions. We examine how well-known logicians Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Rosser collaborated, their individual contributions, and the impact of their work. This investigation includes a joint achievement by Godel and Tarski in forming the Berlin Circle, as well as Godel's development of the incompleteness theorems, Tarski's efforts to define truth, and Rosser's use of the incompleteness theorems. Additionally, we look at Carnap's applications of the incompleteness theorems and the logicians' post-war periods. Further, we explore how these logicians navigated the complexities of working within the German academic system and the challenges of immigrating to the United States during a time of significant social change. Our study is primarily based on previously unpublished materials, including the logicians' personal correspondence, as well as their published works and the recollections of those who knew them. Michler, and it sheds new light on the history of logic, semantics, and the migration of scholars during World War II. This paper formulates the Three Balls Conjecture in terms of the Laplace-Beltrami operator, and provides a proof for its validity. We leverage complex interpolation theory to demonstrate that the conjecture holds true for the Laplace-Beltrami eigenfunctions. Furthermore, we expand on the application of this proof to the Toric variety and polynomial Heisenberg groups. Additionally, the paper explores a related issue with the Hadamard conjecture. Lastly, we offer a modified version of the Three Balls Conjecture tailored to the Dirac operator. This modification enables us to establish a lower bound for the volume of a non-flat component in three-dimensional space. This volume is associated with the second lowest eigenvalue of the Dirac operator, and we prove that it is greater than a specific, albeit very small, fraction of the minimal surface area. This modification is relevant to the highest eigenvalue of the Laplace-Beltrami operator on these types of geometric structures. Although the proposed bound is extremely modest, it raises an interesting question about whether it could be improved with the Hadamard conjecture. We explore this possibility through a technical approach involving Clifford analysis. This approach enables us to establish a connection between the Dirac operator and the Laplace-Beltrami operator, and subsequently prove the proposed bound for the volume of a non-flat component in three-dimensional space. This proof can be applied across a broad range of geometric structures, including polynomial Heisenberg groups and Toric varieties. One of the key implications of this proof is that it sets a lower bound for the eigenvalue of the Dirac operator in these types of structures. This bound is directly related to the surface area of the component and is achieved through the use of modern mathematical techniques, specifically complex interpolation and Clifford analysis. We believe that this proposed bound could provide a foundation for further modifications to the Three Balls Conjecture, and potentially even for the Hadamard conjecture. These modifications could result in more precise lower bounds for the eigenvalue of the Dirac operator in three-dimensional space, and could potentially be applied across a broad range of geometric structures. However, further research is required to fully explore the potential applications of these modifications, as well as the potential for them to be proven or disproven. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the key challenge lies in modeling the posterior distribution which represents all possible restorations. It is even more complicated when the measurements are limited or noisy, common issues in real-world problems. This paper proposes a new approach called the regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, where the model generates a regularized sample from a given data set, based on that data set's characteristics, and is trained using optimization algorithms that account for the complexity of modeling the posterior distribution. By utilizing the Wasserstein distance, this approach handles unbalanced problems and avoids the sensitivity issues associated with other distance metrics. To control overfitting, this model incorporates two regularization techniques, resulting in a more efficient and reliable estimator for the posterior distribution. This leads to a high-quality image restoration method, as demonstrated by our numerical results. Additionally, this model is versatile and easily applicable to various imaging applications. We provide numerical results showing the benefits of this approach over traditional techniques in MRI reconstruction and image compression. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of the algorithm's convergence and the guaranteed performance of the estimator. This guaranteed performance provides an important insight into the optimal regularization parameters, which can be determined analytically, before even considering any experimental data. Finally, we explore an interesting connection between this model and the classic Tikhonov regularization method. This connection reveals that by incorporating additional constraints, Tikhonov regularization can be seen as a conditional GAN with a linear constraint, leading to a more in-depth understanding of both methods. This understanding results in a unified perspective on both techniques, as well as on other imaging applications that can be formulated as constrained optimization problems. This perspective enables us to reformulate these problems as the training of a conditional GAN, providing a data-driven approach to solve these problems. This, in turn, enables the application of deep learning techniques to solve these problems, even when the measurement operator is not easily invertible. This unification paves the way for a vast range of applications of conditional GANs in solving inverse problems in imaging. This includes MRI reconstruction, computed tomography, image compression, blind deconvolution and super-resolution, among others, as well as in other fields that rely on imaging, such as remote sensing, biological sensing, and biological imaging. A novel numerical strategy has been introduced for solving time-harmonic acoustic scattering issues, primarily centered around analyzing the impact of smoothly varying material inhomogeneities on plane waves. This method's efficiency is optimal for high-frequency scenarios and is adaptable across any given frequency $\omega$. The approach relies on two main components: (1) an efficient approximation of the incoming plane wave that utilizes boundary integral calculations, and (2) a dynamic front-collision-oriented mesh refinement technique, both incorporating quasi-optimally sized elements. The development of an explicit error bound for the proposed scheme provides a refined understanding of its performance. Furthermore, the scheme's effectiveness is demonstrated through several examples, featuring moderately complex structures and high-frequency waves with inhomogeneities, resulting in substantially faster computation times compared to traditional fixed-mesh methods. Additionally, an innovative implicit error analysis strategy, leveraging the front-collision-oriented refinement's unique characteristics, yields superior complexity-driven performance modeling. This innovative approach surpasses the conventional quadratic complexity model, revealing that the proposed scheme's complexity behaves as $O(\omega^2)$ when considering the frequency $\omega$. This has significant implications for the scalability of the method, and the associated implementation is made available for the DOLFIN-FENICS framework. This numerical solution strategy holds significant potential for addressing other wave scattering and related problems. We introduce an element-free method for simulating materials with memory that interact based on planar Newtonian forces. A significant innovation of this approach is the use of a boundary integral formulation that can be efficiently resolved using a Cartesian grid for a wide range of domains. This has the benefit of making the method very easy to implement and highly scalable. Additionally, our method does not require the painful steps of developing a mesh geometry. Some of the notable advantages of this method include the absence of an artificially thin boundary layer, no singularity in surface traction, and the ability to simulate both sticky and slippery surfaces. Some key computational benefits include a simple and conservative algorithm, high accuracy in both energy and momentum, and a clear a priori error estimate.
